#1. Survey: Most Organizations Are Not Consistently Measuring AI Value Against Costs

A new study from consulting firm KPMG found that while AI investment continues to grow, relatively few organizations consistently measure whether the technology's benefits justify its costs. The company's Global AI Pulse Q3 2026 report found that 89% of organizations report measurable value from AI, while just 12% consistently assess that value against costs across the organization.

Average planned AI investment for the next 12 months has risen to $210 million, compared with $186 million in the first quarter of 2026.

The findings are based on responses from 2,131 senior leaders across 20 countries and jurisdictions, surveyed between July 23 and August 26, 2026.

Most organizations have established ways to track AI spending: 61% review costs during project approval, and 59% monitor them once systems are operating.

Consistently connecting those costs to value remains less common. Beyond the 12% that do so across the organization, another 26% assess value against costs for most initiatives.

Organizations reporting established AI returns have stronger measurement practices. Among this group, 48% consistently assess value against costs, four times the proportion in the overall survey group.

Cost-monitoring dashboards are also more common among organizations reporting established returns: 77% use them, compared with 43% of those still experimenting.

"The organizations seeing a return did the implementation and the transformation properly: guardrails in place, workforce ready, data cleaned up," said Priya Emmanuel, global head of aIQ at KPMG International. "That is a sequence, not a secret."

Organizations are also developing more formal systems to manage AI deployment.

Fifty-five percent operate a formal AI management layer, which KPMG calls a "harness layer," comprising controls and tools between AI models and business applications.

Security and identity controls, along with data access controls, were the most common capabilities, each reported by 43% of respondents. Model routing, which determines which model handles a particular task, was reported by 23%.

Meanwhile, 53% assign accountability for AI-informed decisions to a named executive, the CEO, or an executive committee.

The proportion reporting significant employee adoption of AI agents rose from 25% in the first quarter to 34% in the third quarter.

Cybersecurity concerns were more common among organizations with mature AI programs.

Half of those reporting established AI returns identified cybersecurity as a barrier, compared with roughly one-third of those still experimenting.

Overall, 86% of respondents said their organizations are adapting their cybersecurity operating models to address AI-accelerated threats.

The report identifies accountability, operational resilience, and cost management as priorities as AI becomes more embedded in business operations.

"Many organizations have made AI models widely available and track their use," said Swaminathan Chandrasekaran, head of the US AI Center of Excellence at KPMG. "But consumption alone is not a strategy."

For the full report, visit the KPMG site.

#3. SailPoint Intros New Capabilities to Address Agentic AI Identity Security Challenge

AI agents are moving from experiments into everyday enterprise environments, but the security controls around them are not keeping pace, according to enterprise identity security company SailPoint. In its latest Horizons of Identity Security report, SailPoint found that 79% of enterprises already have AI agents running in production, while just 2% have deployed identity security tools specifically designed to govern them.

That gap could become harder to ignore as organizations give agents more autonomy. Agents can increasingly access applications, sensitive data, and credentials, and in some cases take actions on a user's behalf, effectively creating a new class of identity that IT and security teams need to manage.

SailPoint, which develops identity security and access governance technology for enterprises, is responding with a collection of new identity security capabilities announced at its Navigate 2026 conference. The company is expanding its Agentic Fabric to discover "shadow AI" agents and provide runtime authorization and controls capable of immediately disabling an agent.

The company also introduced what it calls SailPoint Autonomous Agents, specialized AI agents designed to govern other agents. The security agents can monitor runtime activity, intercept threats, and adjust permissions while allowing legitimate agents to continue operating, SailPoint said.

The idea reflects one of the challenges created by increasingly autonomous AI systems: Traditional human approval processes may not be fast enough to govern software capable of taking large numbers of actions on its own.

"The idea that a security admin is going to review and approve access for a group of autonomous agents making 10,000 tool calls a second isn't just outdated — it's a fantasy," SailPoint CTO Chandra Gnanasambandam said.

Another part of SailPoint's approach focuses on visibility.

New endpoint and browser sensors, along with SIEM and XDR telemetry and non-human identity discovery capabilities, are designed to uncover agents, MCP servers, credentials, tools, and data stores that haven't been brought under an organization's identity program.

The company is also introducing Autonomous Identity Security Posture Management, or A-ISPM, which uses identity information from its Atlas platform to identify dormant accounts, orphaned access, shadow administrators, and other potentially risky access paths. Organizations can then revoke access, disable an identity or AI agent, assign an owner or automate enforcement.

Just-in-Time provisioning is another part of the strategy. Rather than giving people, service accounts, and AI agents permanent access, permissions can be granted when needed and subjected to conditions such as reauthentication or a business justification.

Capabilities across SailPoint's Agentic Fabric, Human Fabric, and Atlas platforms are beginning to roll out globally. A-ISPM and several other announced features are expected in the company's fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.

"Autonomous agents are no longer just experimental copilots; they are becoming the primary execution layer of modern enterprises," SailPoint President Matt Mills said.

For more information, go to the SailPoint site.

#4. Diesel price surge triggers budget workarounds, changes to bus routes

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

One Texas district has already spent $1.1 million of its $1.6 million fuel budget for the entire school year. Here’s how it and others are coping.

Surging diesel fuel costs are adding financial pressure to school districts, forcing them to dip into their reserves, alter transportation routes, limit field trips, negotiate vendor contracts, or adjust their budgets to keep up.

"Many districts first try to absorb costs within their current transportation budget; however, some may have no choice but to transfer funds from other programs, tap reserves, or reduce staff and programs altogether to cover rising fuel costs," said Elleka Yost, director of advocacy and research for the Association of School Business Officials International, in an Oct. 14 email.

Between July and early October, Texas' North East Independent School District had already spent about $1.1 million out of its $1.6 million budget for fuel for the entire school year, according to an Oct. 8 district announcement.

The district purchases 7,000 to 8,000 gallons of diesel a week for buses that travel an average of 16,500 to 17,000 miles a day. As such, the San Antonio district said it expected to exceed the year's fuel budget in six to seven weeks if the high prices of the time continued.

“We’ve got to get creative,” said Bill Harrison, executive director of transportation, in an Oct. 8 statement. “We transport about 15,500 students a day, so they count on our buses to get to school.”

In Texas, diesel prices reached an average of $5.77 as of Oct. 19, according to AAA. That's up from an average $3.11 one year ago. Prices have risen similarly nationwide, with the current average diesel price at $6.32 compared to last year's $3.63.

With cooler weather arriving, NEISD is implementing cost-cutting measures like reducing idling time and waiting until the bell rings to start their engines, instead of cooling off the buses before dismissal.

According to a survey of school district leaders, 56% of respondents said they exceeded their approved or final budget for diesel to some extent in the 2025-26 school year. The survey was administered in May by three groups: ASBO International; AASA, the School Superintendents Association; and the National Association for Pupil Transportation.

In response to rising fuel prices, 40% reported consolidating bus routes, 27% enforcing anti-idling measures, 25% reducing the number of routes, and 20% limiting nonrequired travel like field trips.

Most of the district leaders said they were absorbing extra costs within their current transportation budget or transferring funding from other district programs, but 19% said they were using district reserves/rainy day funds.

"There was no anticipatory reality in the budget," said Noelle Ellerson Ng, chief advocacy and governance officer at AASA.

"And while school district budgets can plan to absorb cuts or can brace in some flexibility if they can anticipate a new variable, rising cost of diesel is not something you can delay," Ellerson Ng said. "You have to absorb it in real time, and that was the biggest disruption in the [20]25-26 school year because you can't not pay diesel."

For the 2026-27 school year, school districts are in a better position to absorb the costs because they've had time to plan, said Ellerson Ng.

In the May survey, a third of respondents said they were looking to build a contingency or reserve for fuel volatility for the 2026-27 school year. However, 37% still said they would have to dip into their rainy day funds, 30% said extracurriculars or athletic activities might face cuts, and over 20% said other categories — such as facilities, non-instructional staffing, professional development or technology — could be affected.

The unanswered question, of course, is what the future will bring as the country faces exponentially rising fuel costs from inflation and the war conflict in Iran.

According to Yost, "Tapping reserves for a temporary unanticipated cost increase isn’t a concern, but sustained reliance on reserves to pay for recurring obligations if fuel costs stay high may signal deeper financial challenges within a district."

The high diesel costs pushing districts to sometimes dip into their reserves are coming at a time when district budgets are already stressed from declining enrollments and various funding changes. For instance, declines at the state level in Medicaid and SNAP have a trickle down effect on districts' qualifications for Title I funds. These changes will also affect what's available in general state budgets, said Ellerson Ng.

"The two biggest drivers of state budgets are health and education," she said. "So it's really likely we're going to see downward trends on state spending in education, particularly starting for the [20]27-28 school year."

Inflation overall is also chipping away at district funding, as rising food, healthcare and labor costs are all thrown into the mix.

"Rising transportation costs are only one aspect of the broader inflationary challenges facing districts," said Yost.

Two-thirds of district leaders said their state doesn’t provide dedicated transportation funding that rises with fuel prices, according to the survey.

"When more funds must be spent on fuel and transportation, it is a huge opportunity cost, as fewer dollars go to students and classrooms," said Yost. "Supplemental state funding for transportation would certainly help districts that are feeling the squeeze on their budgets."

#5. Nearly half of employers say AI will make college degrees more important

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Employers expressed more confidence in the higher education sector than the general public, according to a new Gallup and the Lumina Foundation poll.

Nearly half of surveyed employers — 48% — think higher education will become more important over the next five years amid growing use of artificial intelligence, while only 26% think it will become less important, according to data released Tuesday by Gallup and the Lumina Foundation.

Across industries, large majorities of employers said that college degrees would be at least as important as they are today.

The sector with the largest share of employers who felt degrees would become less important was business and professional services, with 37% saying credentials would be somewhat or much less important. It was followed by leisure and hospitality, with 34%  who said college degrees would become less important.

Across industries and organization sizes, 80% of employers say they prefer candidates with college degrees regardless of the position's requirements, with 31% strongly preferring them.

That preference varies somewhat by size. At companies with fewer than 10 employees, 62% of those in charge of hiring preferred college graduates. At the largest organizations, 86% of employers preferred candidates with degrees.

The report’s authors pointed to widespread speculation about “how artificial intelligence will reshape the labor market and the credentials employers demand.”

“The employers who make those decisions do not, for now, appear to be turning away from the degree,” they wrote.

Tuesday's survey marked the second annual study from Lumina and Gallup on employer sentiment on higher ed. It was based on an August online survey of over 2,500 people who made hiring decisions at their organizations.

#6. Job search advice for every generation: Interview tips from Lorna Erickson

Senior Manager of Strategic Partnerships | Oct 13, 2026

Most interview advice comes from one side of the table. On this episode of "Ask a Recruiter Live," we wanted to flip it.

I sat down with Lorna Erickson, hiring strategist and co-founder of Expert Interviews, who's spent her career training hiring managers to interview better. We talked about how shifting professional norms impact different candidate cohorts during interviews, the bold questions that expose a company's real culture across generations, how to push through a stalled job search, and her no-holds-barred hot takes on hiring habits that need to disappear.

Asking about work-life balance or outside causes in an interview can feel like it'll make you look unprofessional under old-school standards. Lorna pointed to Gen Z career expert Danielle Farage's observation that many younger candidates graduated during COVID and watched their parents live through the 2008 recession. As Lorna put it, "They just weren't really trained on how to be quote-unquote professional, whatever that means."

The Fix: Ask about what matters most to you, and treat a bad reaction as information. What counts as "professional" has shifted across generations, and curiosity about values isn't disqualifying. If an interviewer from a different era treats your question like it was out of line, that tells you something about the company, not about you.

Every company has a polished pitch, the "we're like a family," "amazing culture" version it leads with. Lorna admitted she used to sell candidates on exactly that kind of language early in her own recruiting career, and now hears it as a red flag herself.

The Fix: Ask the question that forces proof, not a pitch. Lorna's go-to: "Walk me through a time when you had to work with an underperformer." She also suggests asking how a company handles low morale. It can be divisive, and some old-school interviewers will mark it against you, but if a company can't answer with an authentic example, that tells you something too.

Applying into the void rarely changes the outcome. Between layoffs, AI-driven hiring, and a flood of applicants for every role, Lorna acknowledged the market right now is genuinely hard.

The Fix: Lean on relationships and rethink traditional career expectations. "I think, eventually, it always comes back to the humans," she said, pointing job seekers toward people they've already worked with instead of another round of cold applications. She also encouraged letting go of the older generation's mindset that a career has to mean one company for 20 years — freelancing, consulting, and shorter stints are legitimate paths now, not detours.

Ghosting and outdated reference checks still get treated as just how hiring works. When I asked her for a hiring trend that needed to die immediately, Lorna didn't hesitate: "ghosting." She added, "How is it possible to still ghost candidates? ... that's absolutely bonkers to me," noting that automations exist specifically to close the loop with candidates.

The Fix: Expect, and push for, basic accountability. Her second hot take landed just as hard: "References need to die." Candidates remember how they're treated, she noted. As she put it, "Your candidates are potentially future clients."

Want Lorna's full take on interviewing from both sides of the table? Watch the full "Ask a Recruiter Live" episode here.

Put this advice to work by trying Glassdoor Recruiter to help you find your job match with companies that are actually transparent about culture, pay, and growth.

1. How do generational differences affect job interviews?Different generations often prioritize distinct values during interviews. For instance, younger candidates like Gen Z frequently ask about work-life balance and company values early in the process. Rather than seeing this as unprofessional, candidates and recruiters should view these questions as useful information about culture alignment.

2. What should you do when your job search has stalled?Instead of submitting more cold applications into online portals, focus on building and leveraging genuine human relationships and former working connections. Additionally, consider alternative career formats such as freelancing, consulting, or project-based work to rebuild momentum.

3.  Why are practices like ghosting and reference checks becoming outdated?Modern hiring experts consider ghosting unacceptable given the availability of automated communication tools to close the loop with candidates. Similarly, traditional reference checks are increasingly viewed as outdated, with more focus placed on transparent evaluation methods and treating applicants with respect as potential future client connections.

#9. Flashpoint Receives Patent for Ransomware Risk Model, Tying Vulnerabilites to Likelihood of Attack

Cybersecurity company Flashpoint announced it has received U.S. Patent No. 12,705,360 for its Ransomware Risk model, a methodology designed to help security teams determine which newly disclosed vulnerabilities more closely resemble those historically used in ransomware attacks.

The patent comes at a time when security teams are confronting a growing vulnerability problem: Flashpoint's Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition tracked 21,667 vulnerability disclosures during the first half of 2026, an 8% increase.

Of those, 4,015, or around 19 percent, already had public or functional exploit code. Flashpoint also reported a 45 percent increase in Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) attacks during the period.

The patent was granted August 11 2026, although the underlying Ransomware Risk model isn't new. It has been available through Flashpoint Vulnerability Intelligence since 2022.

The model addresses a basic vulnerability-management problem: severity and real-world ransomware risk aren't necessarily the same thing, because severity scores do not necessarily indicate which flaws attackers are most likely to target.

The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, or CVSS, measures how severe a vulnerability could be. The Exploit Prediction Scoring System, or EPSS, estimates the probability of exploitation more broadly.

Flashpoint's Ransomware Risk model adds another dimension by comparing newly disclosed vulnerabilities with the characteristics of flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks.

That could change where a vulnerability lands in an organization's patching queue. A lower-severity flaw might normally sit behind numerous critical vulnerabilities. But if its characteristics closely resemble vulnerabilities repeatedly targeted by ransomware operators, security teams may have reason to move it higher.

"A severity score alone can't tell you which vulnerabilities pose the greatest real-world risk of exploitation by ransomware actors," Flashpoint CEO Josh Lefkowitz said. "Our patented Ransomware Risk model applies years of threat intelligence to that problem, giving customers an earlier signal and helping them prioritize based on how attackers actually operate."

The firm's midyear research also illustrates the scale of the prioritization problem. Its vulnerability intelligence covers traditional IT systems as well as cloud, IoT, operational technology, open source software. and third-party libraries.

The company says it also tracks more than 105,000 vulnerabilities that aren't represented in CVE or the National Vulnerability Database, expanding the pool of flaws that security teams may need to evaluate.

The cybersecurity company's patented methodology profiles vulnerabilities using more than 60 technical characteristics, including whether a flaw can be exploited remotely without authentication, whether it affects operational technology systems, and how exploitation could affect data availability.

Those characteristics form a multi-factor fingerprint. The model maps each vulnerability against clusters containing flaws previously exploited in ransomware attacks and assigns a Low, Medium, High, or Critical Ransomware Risk rating.

Flashpoint says the rating can be generated when a vulnerability is disclosed, rather than requiring security teams to wait for public evidence of active exploitation. Ratings are then updated as new ransomware activity and threat intelligence emerge.

Within Flashpoint Ignite, Ransomware Risk appears alongside CVSS, EPSS, Social Risk, and exploit maturity. The idea isn't to replace existing scoring systems, but to give administrators additional information when deciding what to remediate first.

Nor does a High or Critical Ransomware Risk rating mean a vulnerability will necessarily be exploited. The model measures how closely its characteristics resemble vulnerabilities historically associated with ransomware attacks.

For security teams facing thousands of potential vulnerabilities, that distinction matters. The flaw carrying the highest severity score isn't necessarily the one that most closely resembles what ransomware operators have historically chosen to attack.

"Despite being the most popular indicator for priority, we know that severity alone doesn't tell you whether a vulnerability will be exploited or used in ransomware," said Ben Haynes, Data Science & Analytics Lead at Flashpoint and co-inventor of the patented methodology.

"A vulnerability can score low on a traditional severity scale and still share the characteristics we repeatedly see in ransomware attacks."

For more information, go to the Flashpoint site.

#11. Navigating your job search with AI: 5 key insights

Program Manager of Corporate Marketing | Oct 9, 2026

Artificial intelligence (AI) is everywhere at work, and the honeymoon is over. Glassdoor Economic Research found 81% of Glassdoor reviews mentioning AI listed it only as a pro in 2019, versus 43% in 2026.¹ Use AI for job search, but write for humans.

"The key is to focus less on the AI algorithm and more on the human one - i.e., the one running between every recruiter's two ears!" said Jeremy Schifeling, founder of The Job Insiders.

Jeremy Schifeling, expert AI career coach of The Job Insiders, has seen firsthand how AI is reshaping the job search landscape. The author of the AI careers book Career Coach GPT brought his expertise to a Glassdoor Community Hot Seat session, sharing hard-won wisdom from his own career pivots — from teacher to recruiting expert — and the thousands of job seekers he's helped navigate this new terrain.

From AI's biggest pitfalls to the soft skills that will define the next decade of work, here are five of Schifeling's most useful insights to help workers navigate their job search.

Schifeling sees this error everywhere from applicants in today's job market.

"By far the #1 mistake is letting AI turn your unique application into a generic one. When everyone uses AI to write their cover letters and every cover letter begins 'I am writing to express my interest in X role at Y company,' everything that's unique and different about you has just been lost," he said. "That makes it all too easy for the recruiter to reject your application immediately in favor of the handful truly differentiated ones..."

A platform technical lead agreed on Glassdoor Community: "Many recruiters can tell if a cover letter feels generic or doesn't reflect your real experience." Draft with AI, then rewrite using our guides to writing a cover letter and being yourself in a job interview.

When most job seekers are taking the easy route, Schifeling advocates for effort over automation. "Standing out is everything! That means NOT doing what everyone else is doing but instead doing what NO ONE else is willing to do," said Schifeling.

One member on Glassdoor Community has hired hundreds. Their take: "I always gave better credibility that candidate was solid if I knew and respected the referrer."

What does Schifeling think about the future of AI? It flips conventional career wisdom on its head.

"My crystal ball prediction is that, because AI is so good at the hard skills we've all focused on for the last few decades (coding, data, etc.), its emergence will actually make soft skills (empathy, storytelling, relationship-building) the scarce and desirable skillset of the next decade," Schifeling said.

He recommends workers do these two things:

Schifeling reminds us that when everyone can prompt AI to do technical work, the people who can do the uniquely human stuff (reading a room, navigating office politics, inspiring others) become incredibly valuable.

The hiring bar is rising, and Schifeling sees a clear trend emerging.

"While I don't think that white collar jobs are cooked by any stretch, I do think that the hires of the next 5 years won't just be good at their jobs: They'll be good at their jobs plus AI," he said. That means if you're already a great coder or salesperson, you'll be able to stand out by taking your skills to the next level when the hiring bar gets higher.

For professionals stuck on their next move, Schifeling suggests using AI as a thinking partner.

"While it all comes down to what you want out of life (e.g., pay vs. work-life balance), this is something you can actually chat with AI about," said Schifeling. "For instance, you could ask ChatGPT to list the pros and cons of any decision to get a better feel for what that's going to entail. I find that AI, while not as powerful as a coach, can be a good way to break through analysis paralysis!"

#12. How an Indiana district saved $20M — and gave teachers a one-time raise

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

South Bend district’s CFO told ASBO’s annual conference how asking critical questions about outsourcing and healthcare costs led to strategic gains.

PITTSBURGH — In school finance leadership, district business officials can choose to either lead with an accountant's mindset of book keeping and compliance — or proactively zero in on financial strategy, Ahnaf Tahmid, chief financial officer at South Bend Community School Corp. in Indiana, told attendees at the Association of School Business Officials International’s 2026 annual conference.

While accounting responsibilities are still crucial, he said, a financial strategist will go further by also building capacity, finding data-driven efficiencies and leading with a strategic vision that considers students, teachers and taxpayers.

During a Thursday ASBO session, Tahmid shared how leading with a financial strategist approach translated into $20 million in savings for his more than 13,000-student district.

South Bend saved about $20 million a year beginning with the 2026 budget cycle by changing healthcare providers and shifting some outsourced services back to the district, among other things, Tahmid said.

The change in healthcare providers was prompted by a 15% jump in 2025 for its share of employees' health insurance premiums, he said. And the premiums were expected to increase by another 13.5% — or about $3 million — in 2026.

When this kind of thing happens, district business officials can either “accept the fate” and make budget cuts to accommodate rising costs, or they can ask strategic questions about alternatives, Tahmid said. That questioning revealed that it had been decades since South Bend had considered switching health insurance providers, he said.

“Why? Because our benefit consultant would always say, ‘Hey, you are getting the best price, man. I mean, why do you want to switch insurance and mess around with people's health?’” Tahmid said. “So no one batted an eye, and we just followed the status quo.”

In the end, the district did decide to switch its insurance provider and netted lower premiums and deductibles — leading to $10 million in savings for 2026 over what staying with its previous provider would have cost, he added.

In another strategic move, South Bend saved money by terminating a contract with a third-party service provider to manage the district's facilities, Tahmid said. By pivoting to in-house management, the district is saving $5 million annually.

Tahmid added that the district saved another $5 million from consolidating administrative roles, terminating contracts for services that weren't being used, and employing artificial intelligence to reduce administrative costs.

For instance, he said, the district was spending $75,000 per year for a financial dashboard service that only two employees actually logged into in the last year — making it an easy choice to cancel the contract. South Bend also consolidated its transportation routes to save district funds.

Meanwhile, the district was struggling to retain teachers, Tahmid said. Though the district has the fifth-largest teacher workforce out of the state's districts, he said, South Bend ranked 203 of the state's 340 districts for average teacher pay.

“That was shameful, in my opinion,” Tahmid said.

To help remedy the situation, the district used $12 million of its $20 million in savings to give all teachers a one-time $9,000 raise. Not only did that make the district the highest paying one in the region, he said, but teacher vacancies fell to zero at the start of the 2026-27 school year.

The savings — and the resulting bump in teacher pay and retention — were possible because the district embraced a strategic mindset. Leaders asked questions and didn't accept “an inevitable fate” that public school education is automatically “doomed” even when funds are dwindling and enrollment is on the decline, Tahmid said.

#14. Convergence of AI, Quantum Risks Is Impacting Cybersecurity

Recent research from Thales highlights how AI adoption and emerging quantum computing threats are putting pressure on existing security measures. The 2026 Thales Data Threat Report: Quantum & AI Trends, based on responses from 3,120 security and IT management professionals across 20 countries, found that 98% are considering how the two technologies affect each other. Thirty percent reported a significant increase in security budgets specifically for AI.

The research, conducted by 451 Research by S&P Global, examines both the risks and potential benefits of the technologies. Fifty-seven percent believe quantum computing will enhance machine learning, while 54% expect it to enable advanced simulations of complex systems. The security findings span data governance, cloud infrastructure, and preparations for quantum-resistant encryption.

Cloud-based storage, cloud-delivered applications, and cloud management infrastructure were the three most frequently cited asset types targeted by attackers, at 35%, 34%, and 32%, respectively. The report connects that exposure to the large datasets required for AI training and the rapid expansion of AI infrastructure.

Organizations are also looking to cloud providers for protection: 67% reported investing in their cloud provider's AI-specific security tools, compared with 63% using an established security provider. Respondents could identify multiple sources of protection, including startups, large language model providers, and internally developed controls.

Encryption coverage remains incomplete. Only 7% of organizations reported encrypting more than 80% of their sensitive cloud data, while 29% reported encrypting more than 60%. The report's chart puts the average share encrypted at 47% in 2026, down from 51% in 2025.

The findings extend concerns raised in coverage of Thales' 2025 cloud security research, when AI security already ranked second to cloud security in spending priorities and 52% of respondents reported that AI security spending was displacing existing security budgets. The latest report again places AI security second, while its historical comparison shows average sensitive cloud data encryption coverage falling from 51% in 2025 to 47% in 2026.

AI security was the second-highest prioritized security spending category overall, behind cloud security. But protecting data ranked much lower among the measures organizations use to judge AI projects: Reducing or managing risks of data loss or noncompliance placed sixth among seven success criteria, at 35%.

Improving customer experience led those measures at 68%, followed by reducing employee toil through greater task automation at 63%. Meanwhile, poor data quality or initial data governance was the leading inhibitor to AI adoption, cited by 65%; security risks from exposed data followed at 61%. Another 51% cited AI initiatives moving too quickly to be properly secured.

#17. Democratic lawmakers accuse Education Department of ‘frontloading’ grants

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A letter from two key Senate Appropriations Committee members says the agency’s approach is making it easier to cancel funding in future years.

Democratic lawmakers this month accused the U.S. Department of Education of "frontloading" grants — or making multiyear funding available in one lump sum ahead of time rather than funding a larger number of grants over time, as is typical.

This approach has led to the withholding of approximately $630 million in appropriated resources across approximately 35 grant programs, according to a letter sent to U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon by lawmakers from the Senate Appropriations Committee.

"In implementing this policy, the Department is intentionally and sharply limiting the number of new grants it will award, by concentrating funds into fewer grants and withholding significant portions of appropriated resources for use in future budget periods," said U.S. Senators Patty Murray, D-Wash., and Tammy Baldwin, D-Wisc, in the Oct. 13 letter.

Murray is vice chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations, and Baldwin is a ranking member of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies.

If the Education Department had stuck with its traditional approach of funding on an annual basis, the agency could have awarded more than 1,000 grants this year across areas including help for first-generation college students, evidence-based student literacy programs, student mental health supports, education research, and recruiting and preparing teachers, the lawmakers said.

In one example cited, the lawmakers said the department frontloaded grants in the Innovative Approaches to Literacy program. Though the agency announced it would make up to 35 awards using the $30 million in funds earmarked in the fiscal year 2026 appropriations law, it issued only four new awards and set aside $13 million for future years for those grants, Baldwin and Murray said.

“The better question is why would an Administration dedicated to improving literacy outcomes and supporting child care for low-income student parents continue the failed approach of previous Administrations?” said Ellen Keast, communications director for the undersecretary at the Education Department, in an Oct. 14 email to K-12 Dive. “Yes, we are returning education to the states and have furthered that effort by funding the highest-quality grantees that will help kids learn to read and support parents in college.”

However, Baldwin and Murray said the Education Department's new funding approach runs counter to Congressional directives and claimed the department had adopted it to further a goal of eliminating the department and some programs.

The lawmakers' concern over the department's changed funding distribution method comes amid ongoing turbulence over the Trump administration's grant funding cancellations. Many such decisions have been tied to grant recipients' use of diversity, equity and inclusion practices. Multiple lawsuits have stemmed from those cancellations, with judges sometimes ruling them unlawful and requiring the department to backpedal even after the department had already issued new grant funding priorities and awards.

It also comes as the Education Department is trying to codify its controversial approach to terminating grant funding even after those approaches landed the agency in legal hot water. In August, the department proposed a rule that would give itself broad authority to end grants, including "for convenience."

Under the changes, the department could abruptly terminate, discontinue or withhold discretionary funding based on a retroactive review of applications — and whether those applications align with an administration’s changing policies.

If this and other proposed changes from the government go through, Baldwin and Murray said in their Oct. 13 letter, "this means the Department could easily terminate all these frontloaded funds, effectively terminating a large swath of FY2026 funds that Congress appropriated on a bipartisan basis."

#18. Claude Intros Sonnet 5.5 with Model-Switching Cybersecurity Safeguards

Anthropic's new Claude release, Sonnet 5.5, brings cybersecurity safeguards that can change which model handles a request during a Claude conversation. Higher-risk tasks can fall back to Sonnet 5.

According to Anthropic's explanation of model switching, automatic fallback is enabled by default in Claude. Users receive a notice, and the answer is labeled with the model that provided it. The chat then stays on Sonnet 5 unless the user changes the selection.

The company identifies penetration testing and exploit generation among activities that may trigger cybersecurity fallbacks. Source-code vulnerability scanning remains supported. Biology and reasoning-extraction safeguards can block requests outright, rather than route them elsewhere.

The distinction matters operationally. A block stops the request; a fallback allows an attempt to continue with a different model. Neither outcome should be treated as interchangeable with completion by the model the user originally chose.

Anthropic says Sonnet 5.5 generates output more than 30% faster than Sonnet 5 and can reduce cost per task by up to 30%, based on its testing. Token prices remain unchanged.

Those claims describe performance under the company's test conditions. An organization evaluating the service also needs to examine what happens when its own assignments encounter safeguards.

An internal pilot could record how often work is interrupted, whether fallback answers are usable, and when users need help. Such measurements would give buyers a more relevant basis for deployment than assuming every task receives the advertised model's capabilities.

Anthropic has announced plans to expand its Cyber Verification Program with tiered access for Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Mythos models. Its current program guidance explicitly excludes the two new 5.5 models and says the expansion is forthcoming.

Organizations should distinguish those planned arrangements from access available today.

The broader enterprise issue is accountability. When an AI service changes models during an assignment, someone still needs to determine whether the resulting work is suitable. A visible handoff helps, but organizations must decide how employees should respond to it.

For more information on Sonnet 5.5, go to the Anthropic site.

#23. Students vote on how to spend $25K at this New York high school

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Giving students a say also offered a lesson in civics and capital project funding, a New York district administrator told ASBO conference attendees.

PITTSBURGH — Saratoga Springs High School in New York gives its roughly 1,900 students a unique opportunity to decide how to spend $25,000 in district funds to improve their school by letting them participate in a campaigning and voting process.

The idea came about after Joseph Greco, director of personnel development at Saratoga Springs City School District, said he realized that students and local adults alike struggled to understand how capital project funding worked — especially when the district was facing a “lean” budget season. Greco was previously a school business official with the district before entering his current role.

Additionally, he said, students were vandalizing school facilities, which signaled a lack of pride or ownership in their school system. Greco also noted a lack of real-life voter participation from age-eligible students, who he said were nervous to cast a ballot because they were unfamiliar with the process.

Meanwhile, district curriculum leaders and teachers wanted students to develop skills to be effective communicators and global citizens as called for by New York’s portrait of a graduate, Greco said.

“So we partner[ed] together on connecting school finance to authentic civic learning,” Greco said. “So this is kind of checking some multiple boxes here: building transparency, trust and ownership.”

Greco shared more about how the district implemented this program at the high school during a Wednesday presentation at the Association of School Business Officials International’s 2026 Annual Conference & Expo in Pittsburgh.

A key part of the initiative is that students were involved throughout this participatory budget process, Greco said.

The initiative began in September 2025 with the recruitment of students to lead a committee, followed by a student survey of the entire student body to gather ideas for how they’d like to see the $25,000 spent. From there, the student committee helped consolidate and narrow down those ideas in November before meeting with district leaders in December to understand how feasible those ideas are.

After that process, an official ballot was created in January, and students campaigned in February on the top five school improvement projects they’d like to spend the $25,000 on.

In March, the entire student body weighed in using official voting machines to cast their ballots through a ranked voting system. The winning vote was then implemented between April and June, Greco said.

All students in grades 9-12 were eligible to vote on the proposals and did so during their social studies class blocks, he said.

The five improvement projects students had to choose between were: creating bocce courts, buying a grill for the school cafeteria, providing upgraded feminine hygiene products in bathrooms, improving bathroom privacy through facility upgrades, and purchasing new outdoor water bottle dispensers.

The new cafeteria grill was approved by the student body, Greco said, and students were so excited about the outcome that they held a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new grill and provided free samples of grilled chicken.

“It’s a grill, but they still wanted to have a ribbon cutting because they were super excited, because it was their idea,” Greco said, adding that students invited district administrators, local politicians and members of the local chamber of commerce to attend the event.

After the first year of this student budgetary process, Greco said, students now felt more engaged in the voting process, because they got to use official voting machines with volunteer poll workers in their school auditorium.

Before this initiative began, Greco said students “didn't have ownership over the stuff in their building, and they were registering to vote, but they didn't know how to vote, and they weren't participating.” But now, students were “engaging in a huge buildingwide process, and they were seeing that their voice had meaning.”

Greco said that after the district purchased and installed the new grill, there were still some remaining funds from the $25,000 balance to pay for bathroom privacy upgrades, which was the second-most popular proposal that students voted on.

Though there wasn’t any additional funding to cover the cost of new bocce courts, he said, the district’s facilities team changed their budget to install the courts after talking with students who wanted them.

For school leaders looking to launch a similar budgetary process with their students, Greco recommends they secure funds for the initiative before getting students involved. The allocated funds for this program should also be enough to get students excited and involved.

Otherwise, if the amount of funding comes up short for small-scale student capital project proposals, Greco said, “it may lead to disappointment in the process and low participation.”

Saratoga City School District carved out money from its general fund for the initiative, Greco said. While other districts could consider funding a similar project using grants or private donations, Greco urged caution on those types of funding streams, because they can be more unstable.

To get a school board, superintendent and local community to approve of this district budget line item, Greco said school finance officers can say the project will help boost student voice and choice in how district funds are used. On top of that, a student budgetary process is a strong return on investment given that it’s improving student involvement in school and community issues, he said.

“So, for a very small amount of money, you're getting a lot of that additional curricular pieces of that civic readiness of the global citizen,” Greco said.

Greco also suggested that schools look for two teacher advisors to help keep students on schedule and facilitate the process, and there should be an additional stipend to pay for the club advisor positions.

If possible, he said, schools should try to recreate a legitimate ballot to help students have an authentic voting experience. That should include considering an additional cost for the project when printing ballots, securing machines and finding poll workers from the local government.

#24. Inside higher ed’s wave of price resets and free tuition models

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

We’re rounding up recent affordability initiatives — including lower sticker prices and free tuition plans — at a dozen liberal arts colleges.

The cost of college has become eye-watering for many students, driving sectorwide conversations about the value of higher education. But many institutions are quick to distinguish their tuition sticker price from what students actually pay.

Washington College, in Maryland, lists tuition at nearly $60,000 a year. But it says the average student pays less than half that, $28,000, for tuition, fees, housing and food a year.

The private liberal arts institution announced last month that it will cover tuition for new full-time students from Maryland whose families make $75,000 a year or less.

Undergraduate Sticker Price: $58,704 for new students in 2026-27

Free tuition eligibility: Maryland students whose families make $75,000 a year or less

Large, well-heeled universities first popularized this kind of tuition pledge. But smaller colleges and those without massive endowments, like Washington, are increasingly turning to these kinds of affordability initiatives.

A recent Brookings Institution report found that many types of institutions — including public four-year colleges and those with large endowments — already award enough financial aid on average to cover tuition to students from households in the bottom quarter of the income distribution nationwide. The exception was private tuition-dependent colleges.

Additionally, Levine didn't find evidence free tuition policies made a big impact on net college prices for students at this income level.

"For many students, free tuition policies may function less as new aid than as a repackaging of existing aid into a more salient form," Phillip Levine, a senior fellow at Brookings and author of the report, said in the analysis. "While free tuition may not correspond to additional aid, these policies can help communicate to eligible students that they will not need to pay the full sticker price."

At least half a dozen colleges announced last month that they would offer no-cost tuition to certain students.

In Ohio, Denison University students entering in fall 2027 will pay nothing for tuition if their families make $100,000 a year or less. The liberal arts institution also announced a tiered pricing system for students that don't qualify for free tuition.

Undergraduate sticker price: $74,000 for 2026-27

Free tuition eligibility: New students whose families make $100,000 a year or less

Families making just over $100,000 to $200,000 will pay no more than 5% of their income toward tuition. For those earning between $200,001 and $300,000, Denison will cap tuition at 10% of their income. Beyond that, students whose families make up to $400,000 annually will pay at most 15% of their income toward tuition.

The median household income nationwide was about $87,500 in 2025, according to U.S. Census Bureau data. Just 16% of U.S. households made $200,000 or more in 2024.

Before the initiative, Denison had already pledged to fully cover a student's demonstrated need.

Adam Weinberg, the college's president, framed Denison's new initiative as a way to bring transparency to its pricing. In a statement, he said families often don't know the extent of aid they could receive at Denison and that the new program "provides clarity earlier" in the application process.

Some small institutions have launched state-specific versions of these programs.

Starting with its fall 2027 entering class, Earlham College will guarantee that Indiana students pay no tuition if their annual household income is $100,000 or less. Newberry College has the same offer for first-time and transfer students from South Carolina.

Undergraduate sticker price: $56,784 for 2026-27

Free tuition eligibility: New Indiana students whose families make $100,000 a year or less

Undergraduate sticker price: $29,400 for 2026-27

Free tuition eligibility: New and transfer on-campus students from South Carolina whose families make $100,000 a year or less

Newberry specified that its initiative is a last-dollar aid program, meaning it will cover the remaining cost of tuition after a student's federal and state aid and scholarships are applied.

The $100,000 cut-off for both offers could cover large swaths of the population in both states. In Indiana, the median household income in 2024 was just under $72,000, according to Census data. In South Carolina, it was just over $69,000.

Wellesley College, in Massachusetts, and Middlebury College, in Vermont, each announced free tuition programs last month. Wellesley set its income cap at $200,000 while Middlebury will extend the offer to new students whose families earn $175,000 or less annually. The colleges had endowments worth $3.2 billion and $1.7 billion, respectively, in fiscal 2025, NACUBO and Commonfund data shows.

Undergraduate sticker price: $72,924 in 2026-27

Free tuition eligibility: New students whose families make $175,000 a year or less

Undergraduate sticker price: $72,570 in 2026-27

Free tuition eligibility: Students whose families make $200,000 a year or less

The endowments of most of these colleges surpass the national median of $253.6 million, according to data from Commonfund and the National Association of College and University Business Officers.

But they are still significantly smaller than those at the private universities that popularized the free-tuition model.

In contrast, Harvard University had an endowment worth $55.7 billion in fiscal 2025. In 2004, the institution began covering tuition and room and board for students whose families made $40,000 or less annually. Harvard has since raised that cap to $100,000. Families who make $200,000 or less a year do not have to pay tuition.

Likewise, Princeton University, which has offered free tuition, room and board to students from households making $65,000 or less since 2016, had an endowment worth $36 billion. Princeton has since upped the offer's income cap to most families earning $100,000 or less.

Institutions that limited their free-tuition policies by residency as well as household income had the smallest endowments of the group. Washington College had a $350 million endowment in fiscal 2025, while Earlham's endowment was $427.8 million the same year, according to NACUBO and Commonfund.

Other small colleges are overhauling their sticker prices altogether. This move, known as a tuition reset, typically sees a college slash its published price to an amount more in line with what the average student pays and commensurately decrease the institutional aid it awards.

Carroll College said last month that it will cut its listed tuition by 40% to $26,800 in the 2027-28 academic year. Based on its sticker price, the Catholic institution is currently the most expensive college in Montana, it said in the announcement.

Original undergraduate sticker price: $44,712 for 2026-27

New undergraduate sticker price: $26,800 for 2027-28

Like colleges pursuing the free tuition model, Carroll said its tuition reset is meant to show prospective families that attendance is more financially attainable than they may think.

"The new model gives families a clearer understanding of Carroll’s cost, making it easier to compare their college choices and see Carroll as a realistic option," the college said in its announcement. "A more transparent starting point also allows families to explore financial aid and plan for college with greater confidence."

Carroll will continue to offer scholarships and financial aid, though at a level calibrated to its new price. On its website, the college said that the tuition reduction would not necessarily result in current students paying less and noted that the average institutional aid package it awards to full-time students already takes about 45% off its listed price.

Carroll will also eliminate its general student fees for undergraduates, which are about $1,450 a year.

Original undergraduate sticker price: $27,200 for 2026-27

New undergraduate sticker price: $21,700 for 2027-28

In Minnesota, one college is resetting its tuition for the second time in under 15 years. Concordia University St. Paul will cut its sticker price by about 20% in the 2027-28 academic year. Its new published tuition price, $21,700, will match what it was in the 2007-08 academic year and be about 40% less when adjusted for inflation, according to the college.

Concordia cited its first tuition reset, in 2013, as a driving force behind the enrollment growth it experienced in the years that followed — up 98.9% from 3,018 students in fall 2012, the year before the reset, to 6,003 in fall 2024, according to federal data.

Original undergraduate sticker price: $58,780 for 2026-27

New undergraduate sticker price: $31,850 for 2027-28

In neighboring Iowa, Coe College will also slash its sticker price by nearly 46% to $31,850 for the 2027-28 academic year. The liberal arts college already caps direct costs — which include tuition, housing and meals — for in-state students at about $25,600 in a bid to compete with Iowa's public universities.

Beyond broad free tuition promises and sticker price resets, a handful of colleges have announced other types of affordability initiatives.

In Connecticut, Trinity College is going hyperlocal. The liberal arts college will provide free tuition and room and board to students from the surrounding city of Hartford, which has about 122,000 people. Just over 22% of locals 25 years and older hold a bachelor's degree, according to Census Reporter.

Undergraduate sticker price: $72,820 for 2026-27

Less than 100 miles west, Marist University announced it will cap annual tuition and room and board costs at $32,000 for new students from New York if their families make $200,000 a year or less.

Undergraduate sticker price: $50,760 for 2026-27

Policy: New students from New York whose families make $200,000 a year or less

The university said the program is designed to give "eligible New York families access to a private university education at a price competitive with New York’s leading public universities" — a nod to the State University of New York system.

The median household in New York made about $80,000 in 2023, according to the Federal Reserve of New York, though income varies significantly across the state. In Long Island, for example, that number was 63.4% higher at $131,000.

Even so, roughly 83% of New York families would qualify for Marist's plan, according to data from Census Reporter.

And beginning fall 2027, Carleton College, in Minnesota, will eliminate loans as part of its financial aid packages. It is the first in the state to do so, according to the liberal arts college, and joins the ranks of just a handful of institutions, including Dartmouth College and Princeton and Harvard universities.

Undergraduate sticker price: $75,186 for 2026-27

Policy: No loan as part of financial aid packages

Despite its annual tuition sticker price over $75,000, Carleton says that families receiving need-based aid paid an average of just under $22,000 in 2026-27.

#25. Survey Identifies Data Governance Enforcement Gap for Agentic AI Tools

According to a new survey from identity security company Delinea, 99.7% of IT and security leaders said their organization has a formal policy governing what data AI tools and agents are permitted to access. Yet only about 51% said AI access is checked against those policies in real time. Perhaps more worrying is that only 19% said their organization could detect in real time when an agent last accessed data outside its intended scope.

That disconnect is at the center of Delinea's fall 2026 Identity Security Report, "The AI Enforcement Gap," which suggests companies have made quick progress establishing AI governance but have not necessarily built the technical controls needed to enforce it.

The findings come from a pair of surveys covering 2,254 IT and security leaders and 2,250 non-IT employees at organizations with at least 500 employees across the U.S, U.K, Germany, Australia, Singapore, UAE, France, and India.

All the organizations were using or piloting AI, while the employees surveyed used at least one AI tool for work.

The problem becomes more consequential as companies move from AI tools that primarily respond to users toward agents capable of taking actions on their behalf.

Eighty-seven percent of IT and security respondents said their organization had experienced or suspected of an incident during the past year in which an AI tool or agent accessed sensitive information beyond what was required for its task.

Delinea's research also suggests companies are giving agents access that can persist longer than necessary. Only 58% of IT and security leaders said they have mechanisms that automatically revoke or expire AI access when a session ends, and those controls do not necessarily cover every agent or tool. Forty-two percent said many agent credentials remain active until an audit.

Agents also are not always receiving their own narrowly defined permissions. Half of IT leaders said their organizations use the employee's existing permissions as a boundary for what an agent can access. That can effectively hand an agent years of accumulated access belonging to the person who launched it.

That is particularly significant because an AI agent does not necessarily behave like a traditional service account. A service account typically performs a predefined process, while an agent can choose different tools, actions and sequences at runtime depending on the situation.

"Service accounts run fixed scripts," said Mike Albrecht, associate director in the Risk Advisory Practice at Cross Country Consulting. "An AI agent decides what actions it's going to take at runtime."

The enforcement problem is not limited to autonomous agents.

The researchers found that 76% of employees surveyed had bypassed formal approval at some point to use AI tools with company data, applications or systems. And 48% said they always or extensively use AI tools without going through formal approval.

Meanwhile, 60% said they had felt pressure to use AI with sensitive or confidential information even when they were not sure doing so was permitted.

Executives were particularly likely to circumvent the process. Eighty-one percent of C-level respondents said they always or regularly bypass AI access approval, compared with 33% of intermediate-level employees.

The result is a widening gap between written AI governance and what companies can see and control. Delinea found that only 41% of IT leaders said all AI tools and agents accessing company data are actively monitored. When an AI tool or agent went outside its intended scope, 55% said it took at least a day to detect the incident, while 30% said detection took four days or longer.

That suggests the next phase of enterprise AI governance may depend less on writing additional rules and more on whether organizations can enforce existing ones while an agent is working.

"Most organizations cannot confidently answer three questions: What agents are running in our environment? What can they access? What have they actually done?" said Delinea CEO Art Gilliland. "An agent can begin a session with legitimate access and drift into something it was never meant to do."

The full report is available for download here.

#30. OpenAI Intros Dots, AI Agents that Continue Working Between User Conversations

OpenAI has introduced Dots, GPT-6 Astra-powered agents that run on their own cloud computers, using connected applications to carry on with assignments between conversations and incorporating users' feedback as they go.

OpenAI is also previewing specialist Dots for organizations, with separate identities and credentials for defined responsibilities. Those enterprise deployments are beginning with focused pilots. The company is working with Microsoft on integration with Agent 365's governance and security controls.

The broader ambition seems to be to make delegation last beyond a chat session. That change could reduce the need to repeatedly explain a project. It also makes supervision a continuing obligation: An instruction that was appropriate yesterday may no longer fit today's circumstances.

One important distinction appears in OpenAI's privacy and safety FAQ. Disconnecting an application stops new access through that connection, but does not delete information already incorporated into a Dot's context.

Users currently cannot inspect or directly edit individual Dot memories. Deleting a Dot deletes its own context, while files and conversations it created remain separately stored. Plugin permissions are shared across Dots, ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex.

For an organization, that creates two related governance questions: what an agent can retrieve now, and what it already knows. Revoking a connection addresses the first without necessarily resolving the second.

OpenAI's safety account distinguishes authorized tasks that continue in the background from unsolicited "proactive research." The latter uses tools restricted to reading permitted sources. Those research tasks cannot directly send messages, change connected application content, or control a browser or desktop. Any subsequent action must pass the usual rules and checks.

A separate system, Auto-review, checks certain planned actions against instructions and safety requirements. OpenAI says the agent cannot modify the controls enforcing those checks.

"Dots can still make mistakes," the company cautions.

OpenAI's Dots system-card appendix acknowledges that persistence and multi-agent systems are not new. Its evaluations examine how continuing work affects authorization boundaries.

In one test involving successive related tasks, moderate scope violations increased from 8.6% to 19.7% when the number of intervening tasks doubled from five to 10. Examples included carrying information between unrelated tasks or editing a shared document beyond the intended scope. The company reported no severe breaches or exfiltration in that evaluation.

These are controlled test results, not measured failure rates in customer deployments. They nevertheless identify a problem that a successful demonstration cannot settle: whether an agent keeps the right boundaries as its workload accumulates.

According to OpenAI's DevDay recap, Dots are available to Pro and Business Premium users in eligible markets. Enterprise, Edu, and Healthcare access is an administrator-enabled beta, off by default.

The operational question is how organizations will keep delegated authority current. A continuing assignment needs a human owner who can revise its scope and decide when to stop it. Otherwise, the convenience of leaving work with an agent can outlast the reason it was authorized.

For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

#35. 50 common interview questions and answers

Glassdoor sifted through tens of thousands of interview reviews to find out some of the most common interview questions candidates are getting asked in recent interviews.

Glassdoor Team | Author & Career Expert at Glassdoor | Oct 7, 2026

Glassdoor sifted through tens of thousands of interview reviews to find out some of the most common interview questions candidates are getting asked in recent interviews.

Candidates are holding on to the offers they get, which makes every interview precious and each of these common interview questions worth practicing. Job offer decline rates fell to 21.4% for interviews that began between January 1 and April 15, 2026, according to Glassdoor Economic Research¹. That's down 5.1 percentage points from the same period last year.

Daniel Zhao, Glassdoor's chief economist, told CNBC Make It that "there's no time like the present" to practice your interviewing skills. One of the best ways to get ready for a virtual job interview is to practice your responses to the most common interview questions.

We've sifted through tens of thousands of interview reviews to find out some of the most common interview questions candidates get asked during recent interviews. If you have a job interview lined up, practice in front of a mirror or ask a friend or family member to listen to your answers to the following questions, so you’ll be ready to put your best foot forward. We’ve broken all 50 questions down into 10 categories.

Focus: These questions help establish first impressions and allow interviewers to understand your basic motivations and fit.

What they’re looking for: Interviewers want to hear a confident elevator pitch that proves you are prepared and can communicate your professional value concisely.

General advice: Keep your responses concise and purposeful (under 90 seconds). Use the "Present-Past-Future" framework: describe your current role, briefly explain relevant experience, and connect your goals to this specific opportunity. Research the company thoroughly beforehand so you can speak authentically about why you're interested.

Focus: These questions ask you to differentiate yourself and articulate your unique contributions.

What they’re looking for: They want to see if you understand the company’s specific problems and if you have the quantifiable skills to solve them.

General advice: Use specific examples and quantifiable achievements. Align your strengths with the job description's key requirements. When discussing what you'd accomplish, show you've researched the role and understand immediate priorities. Avoid generic answers — specificity demonstrates preparation and genuine interest.

Daniel Zhao's advice in CNBC Make It: show hiring managers you're "one of the top 10 candidates that they have seen out of potentially 100."

Focus: These questions assess your ability to self-reflect, learn from mistakes, and pursue continuous improvement.

What they’re looking for: They are testing for emotional intelligence and your ability to take accountability for growth rather than hiding your flaws.

General advice: Choose real weaknesses that won't disqualify you, and always follow up with concrete steps you're taking to improve. Frame mistakes and failures as learning experiences with clear takeaways. Avoid clichés like "I'm a perfectionist." Authenticity and self-awareness are valued more than false humility.

One director of talent development on Glassdoor Community summed up weakness questions this way: "This question is about self-awareness. No one is perfect. Do you know enough about yourself to understand your opportunities to develop?"

Related: Glassdoor Community users share the most difficult interview questions they’ve ever been asked

Focus: These questions explore your career path, motivations for change, and long-term vision.

What they’re looking for: They want to ensure your past decisions make sense and that this role is a logical, long-term fit for your future goals.

General advice: Stay positive when discussing previous employers: focus on what you're moving toward, not what you're running from. For employment gaps, be honest and brief, then pivot to what you learned or how you stayed productive. When discussing future goals, balance ambition with realism and show how this role fits your trajectory.

Focus: These questions use past behavior to predict future performance, requiring specific examples from your experience.

What they’re looking for: They use your past actions as the most reliable predictor of how you will handle high-stakes situations in their environment.

General advice: Use the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result). Be specific with context, explain your thought process, detail the actions you took, and quantify results when possible. Choose examples that showcase skills relevant to the job. Prepare 5-7 versatile stories that can be adapted to different questions.

Focus: These questions reveal your intrinsic motivators, personality, and cultural fit.

What they’re looking for: They are determining if your intrinsic drivers and personality align with the team's culture and daily pace.

General advice: Be genuine while staying professional. Connect personal motivators to professional performance when possible. For questions about discomfort or pet peeves, avoid sounding inflexible or difficult to work with. Show self-awareness about what energizes you and how you maintain work-life balance.

Focus: These questions assess how you work with others, lead teams, and navigate workplace relationships.

What they’re looking for: They are gauging your interpersonal maturity and whether you can effectively collaborate, influence others, or manage conflict.

General advice: Demonstrate flexibility. Good employees can both lead and follow depending on context. Use specific examples of successful collaboration or leadership. When discussing others (bosses, direct reports), remain diplomatic and focus on what you learned from different management styles. Show emotional intelligence and maturity.

Focus: These questions test whether you've researched the company and understand the competitive landscape.

What they’re looking for: This is a "seriousness test" to see if you have done the deep research required to contribute from day one.

General advice: Research is non-negotiable. Know the company's products, services, recent news, leadership team, competitors, and market position. Visit their website, read recent press releases, and read Glassdoor company reviews from current and former employees. This preparation demonstrates genuine interest and seriousness about the opportunity.

Some company questions, like "What would you change about our product?", test diplomacy as much as research. As a Domotz employee on Glassdoor Community warned, "It is a minefield of a question because you have no way of knowing how the interviewer will react to your comments."

Focus: These questions address the practical aspects of employment and ensure you’re aligned on basic requirements.

What they’re looking for: They are checking for deal-breakers regarding salary and logistics to ensure both parties are aligned before an offer.

General advice: Be honest about your limitations and flexibility. For salary, research market rates thoroughly (using resources like Glassdoor Salaries) and provide a range rather than a specific number. If possible, try to defer detailed salary negotiations until you have an offer. Know your dealbreakers before the interview so you can respond authentically.

Focus: These questions give you the opportunity to demonstrate curiosity, fill gaps, and leave a strong final impression.

What they’re looking for: They are evaluating your intellectual curiosity and how strategically you assess the business based on the questions you ask.

General advice: Always have 3-5 thoughtful questions prepared that show genuine interest in the role, team, company culture, and growth opportunities. Avoid questions that can be easily answered by the website. Use this as a chance to address any concerns you sensed during the interview or to highlight strengths you haven't yet discussed. Never say "No, I think you covered everything" — this can signal a lack of interest or preparation.

Don't let one stumble rattle you. A district manager on Glassdoor Community explained why: "I don't think I have ever decided not to hire anyone based on this question. Or any single question in particular, really. It is always about the person as a whole."

For more real interview stories, browse the Job Seeker Support bowl.

Trade practice answers with people facing the same interview questions: Join the Glassdoor Community.

How do I find interview questions for a specific company or role?

Search the company's interview reviews on Glassdoor to see the questions recent candidates reported. Reviews also show how candidates rated the difficulty and their overall experience.

What should I do if I get a question that isn't on this list?

Pause, ask a clarifying question if you need one, and adapt one of your prepared stories to the new prompt. Then connect your answer back to the skills the role requires.

Can I use artificial intelligence (AI) to practice common interview questions?

Yes, use AI tools to generate practice questions and pressure-test your drafts, then say each answer out loud in your own words. Over-scripted answers sound rehearsed, so treat AI output as raw material for your own phrasing.

#36. Research: Lack of Specialized Infrastructure Is a Top AI Adoption Challenge

Enterprise AI projects are running into infrastructure questions as organizations move from planning toward deployment, according to recent research Digital Realty. Forty percent of survey respondents cited a lack of specialized infrastructure required by AI as a main challenge to adopting a formal AI strategy, up from 9% in the company's 2024 research.

The Global Data Insights Survey 2026 points to a widening mix of infrastructure models behind enterprise AI. Half of respondents host AI models in private clouds, 86% are pursuing or exploring sovereign AI, 92% tie data-location strategy to their AI plans, and 88% follow a distributed-data approach.

The research is based on an online survey of 2,131 IT decision-makers across 19 countries, and 11 industries, conducted from Nov. 23, 2025, through Feb. 4, 2026.

Organizations also appear to be shifting from AI planning toward execution. The share actively executing AI to achieve operational efficiency or reduce costs rose from 27% in 2024 to 37% this year. Only 3% reported no measurable ROI to date, while 63% expect returns within the next six months to two years.

Specialized infrastructure led the survey's list of AI adoption challenges at 40%, followed by regulatory and personal-data concerns at 35%. Data availability and quality, storage capacity, interconnection, compute resources, and staffing also ranked as significant constraints.

Those requirements are also shaping workload placement. Integration with existing IT or data infrastructure ranked first at 43%, while regulatory compliance and performance were each cited by 37%. Data proximity, sovereignty, sustainability, cost, and intellectual property protection also factored into hosting decisions.

Private cloud features prominently across the report's AI hosting categories, but enterprises are clearly using a mix of private cloud, public cloud, on-premises infrastructure, and colocation. Private cloud accounted for 50% of custom-built AI model hosting and 47% for open source or fine-tuned large language models (LLMs).

Sovereignty is another part of that placement decision. Thirty-two percent consider sovereign AI — in which data and AI models remain within a single national or regulatory jurisdiction — a requirement, while another 54% are exploring it. The findings point toward hybrid environments in which infrastructure location, governance and data control increasingly overlap.

Artificial intelligence is raising the stakes of cyber conflict as attackers use the technology to accelerate reconnaissance, uncover vulnerabilities, and launch attacks faster than many security teams can respond, according to a new report from agentic AI security company Kai.

Cloud Security Alliance's 2026 Top Threats report ranks identity as the leading cloud security concern, followed by two new AI-related risks.

Anthropic announced it is introducing machine-readable watermarks to text generated by supported Claude models as it moves to comply with European Union AI transparency rules.

AI agents have moved into mainstream enterprise use, but the content infrastructure needed to support them has struggled to keep up, according to a new report from cloud content management company Box.
