#39. Educators who use AI say it frees up time to interact with students

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

While AI has become increasingly popular among teachers, professional development over the technology’s use has been less consistent.

Of the educators who said they used AI tools in the 2025-26 school year, 51% said the technology freed up "somewhat more time" for the parts of teaching that matter most to them. Teachers value helping a student work through something they find difficult, seeing students perform well academically, and giving students individual feedback on their work.

Completing administrative or required paperwork ranked lowest among teachers' preferred activities.

The survey was based on responses collected between the end of July and middle of August from more than 1,900 educators.

The findings come as more teachers and students alike seem to be embracing AI, and also as leaders set restrictions and guardrails around the technology’s use.

A survey released in July by Instructure, an ed tech company, showed that AI was becoming more commonplace in schools, with 68% of educators reporting its use at least occasionally and 73% of parents saying their children used it at least occasionally.

That compares to just two years ago, when a 2024 Rand Corp. survey found only 18% of teachers saying they used AI tools in their classrooms.

Despite the reported uptick in teacher usage, districts have been considering or implementing restrictions on AI when it comes to students.

New York City, for example, announced in September what it called the nation’s “most expansive” artificial intelligence moratorium for students. The one-year moratorium prohibits student-facing AI tools for New York City Public Schools students in its preschool program for 2-year-olds through its 8th grade classrooms during the 2026-27 school year.

The temporary AI ban will affect 600,000 students — or two-thirds of NYC’s public school enrollment.

No similar restrictions have been announced for teachers, however. And as teachers increasingly use the technology, professional development may be lagging.

A separate survey released in May by Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation found that over 60% of teachers report receiving no guidance on how to apply artificial intelligence to parts of their jobs, such as analyzing patterns in student learning, tutoring, one-on-one instruction.

Another nearly 60% said they lacked any guidance on how to use AI to grade or provide student feedback, or to supplement instruction. And just under 50% reported receiving no guidance on how to use AI to create assignments and other class materials, or how to modify materials to meet students’ needs.

#42. 9 must-have words to use in a resume

Glassdoor Team | Author & Career Expert at Glassdoor | Oct 7, 2026

Before you call yourself a "rockstar" or pitch your "synergy" one more time, think twice. Clichés don't show what you did.

The right words to use in a resume show your impact before anyone picks up the phone. Proofread, too, since typos distract from your strengths.

"The words used show what level the candidates are at in their career," says job search expert Susan Joyce. "If I picked up a resume for a C-suite candidate who chose vague descriptives, they would immediately be discredited."

Based on expert research, here are nine words key words to include on your resume.

Job coach Angela Copeland says, "Rather than stating that you're an 'excellent digital marketer,' prove it." Her example: "Grew online sales and revenue by 200% in one year."

A recruiter on Glassdoor Community flagged one resume as "lacking context - achievements, outcomes, scope, size, budget of all projects and teams you've been on." Add those details to your work experience section.

Life and career coach Jenn DeWall favors action verbs that show leadership and transformation. "'Redesign' demonstrates problem-solving skills as well as the ability to think big picture and reduce process inefficiencies."

If clichés are a no-no, simple yet powerful words are your go-tos. Simple, practical words that show responsibility carry real weight: launched, solved, transformed, and optimized.

According to master resume writer Jacqui Barrett-Poindexter, modernized, along with "conceived and metamorphosed," is "like a switch, powering up the candidate's story." They show "how they've improved, envisioned and transformed their work environments."

"These words show that the candidate is thinking about their own activities in terms of how they'll improve the business," says author Josh Doody. "Terms like 'hard-working' don't do this because working hard doesn't necessarily produce better results."

"Anyone can say they 'led' a team," insists Joyce. "… Consider the verb 'orchestrated' and how it shows, versus just telling, the hiring manager what was accomplished."

Show you owned the work, says executive coach Kate O'Sullivan. She looks for "candidates who have had a role in shaping something from idea all the way through execution."

A resume is not the time to be shy, says Copeland. "If you were instrumental in a project, replace the word 'helped' with the word 'spearheaded.'"

It shows dedication, start to finish, says DeWall. "Managers can gauge aptitude, readiness, and even your leadership skills from paper."

These five habits help your resume wording land.

Skip the latest buzzword and get specific, Joyce says. "It is important to use verbs that really pinpoint what was accomplished, i.e., influenced, improved, achieved, etc."

O'Sullivan says "it's very hard to convince a resume reader that you possess various soft skills… just by listing these." For teamwork, cite "onboarding new hires or developing a cross-training program."

"Demonstrate those skills in the examples you list for each job/role/title don't list them out separately," said one associate director on Glassdoor Community. See hard skills vs. soft skills.

The Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM) 2025 Talent Trends survey found 43% of HR professionals used AI for HR tasks in 2025. That's up from 26% in 2024, and reviewing or screening applicant resumes is one of the common uses, SHRM reported.

Pull the posting's exact skill terms into your bullets where they're accurate. A Glassdoor Community member wrote that "tailoring your resume to each job—using the exact language from the posting—can help you beat the bots." Swap screening tips in the Job Seeker Support bowl.

"Hiring managers don't sit down the day before an interview," says Doody. Instead, they "open up the resume as the interview is starting and skim it."

On a resume, "every single word counts," says O'Sullivan. "Edit with the mindset of 'Does this piece of information directly help sell my experience for this role?'"

"The easiest way to improve your choice of words is to read your resume out loud to yourself," advises Copeland.

Join the Glassdoor Community to trade resume feedback with people hiring in your field.

Do the same resume words work for director or executive roles?

Use it to spot a posting's repeated keywords, then edit every line so it's true. As one manager on Glassdoor Community put it, make sure "it's still accurate and true to your skills and experience."

#43. AI Ambitions Are Running Into a Network Infrastructure Trust Problem

Enterprise ambitions around AI are running into a fundamental problem: Orgnanizations aren't always confident in the networks those projects depend on, according to a report from telecommunications provider Arelion.

The research found that concerns about network providers have caused organizations to rethink strategic initiatives over the past two years. Among respondents whose initiatives were affected, AI and data-driven projects were the most cited, at 49%. That put AI ahead of security and compliance programs at 44%, digital transformation at 42%, and cloud migration at 38%.

The findings come from Arelion's report, "The Trust Illusion: Why AI and Digital Transformation Need More Than a Reliable Network," based on a survey of 518 senior enterprise network decision-makers in the U.S., U.K., Germany, and France conducted by Savanta.

All respondents worked for organizations with more than 2,000 employees and influenced network strategy across data centers, cloud, and connectivity. Of those surveyed, 66% had final sign-off responsibility. The results suggest that as organizations pursue increasingly data-intensive AI projects, confidence in the network infrastructure supporting them could become another deployment obstacle.

On the surface, Arelion found little evidence of a trust crisis. A total of 93% of respondents said they largely or completely trust their current network provider, while 83% said that trust has strengthened over time.

The picture changes when respondents are asked about a serious network incident. Only 15% said they have complete confidence in their provider's ability to quickly detect and address such a problem. Another 42% said their provider seriously lets them down anywhere from a few times a year to monthly or more frequently.

Those concerns have consequences beyond the network itself. Responding organizations have delayed, scaled back, or stopped strategic initiatives because of provider trust concerns, while others have added resiliency or risk-mitigation measures.

AI and data projects were the most affected among respondents reporting an impact, as organizations try to move AI from experimentation into larger production deployments.

A serious provider failure could also have substantial consequences. Forty percent of respondents said such an event would cause major operational disruption, while 18% anticipated significant financial loss or severe financial or reputational damage.

Another tension runs through Arelion's findings. Enterprises need networks they can trust to support AI projects, but many of the same decision-makers are concerned about AI's growing role inside those networks. A total of 54% of respondents identified AI and automation in network management and security as the factors most likely to negatively affect network trust over the next three years. That ranked ahead of data sovereignty expectations and geopolitical instability, both at 39%, and regulatory requirements and quantum computing threats to current encryption standards, both at 38%.

At the same time, respondents aren't rejecting AI as a network technology. Proactive AI-driven fault prediction was among the capabilities they said would matter most to future trust, alongside stronger built-in security, greater accountability, and responsive support. That leaves enterprises in an unusual position: AI is increasing their dependence on digital infrastructure while also raising questions about how that infrastructure itself is managed.

Arelion has an interest in emphasizing the importance of network-provider trust, and the survey reflects the views specifically of network decision-makers at large enterprises. Still, the findings point to an infrastructure consideration that can get lost amid the rush to adopt new AI models and agents. AI projects ultimately depend on the networks, cloud environments, data centers, and connectivity beneath them. If organizations lack confidence in that foundation, access to better AI models alone won't remove the obstacle.

"Trust is influencing which strategic initiatives move forward, how organizations manage risk, and which providers they choose to work with," said Mattias Fridström, Vice President at Arelion. "As businesses become increasingly reliant on digital infrastructure, enterprises are looking for network providers that can demonstrate transparency, accountability, and operational excellence, not just availability."

The full report is available for download here at the Arelion site (registration required)

#47. OpenAI Getting Rid of Custom GPTs and Moving to Plugin Architecture

OpenAI has announced it will retire Custom GPTs and move the specialized workflows built around them to a new plugin architecture spanning ChatGPT and its Codex coding agent.

Custom GPT retirement is currently scheduled for Dec. 11, 2026, although the company says timing and migration availability can vary by account and workspace.

For affected Enterprise workspaces, OpenAI's current migration schedule targets Oct. 26 for ending creation of new Custom GPTs. Qualifying Enterprise customers with approved deferrals can continue using them until Feb. 11, 2027.

OpenAI has changed its UI to make GPTs less prominent, and when users choose to try creating a new Custom GPT, they are now prompted with an option to create a plugin instead.

Rather than maintaining separate customized versions of ChatGPT, OpenAI is shifting customization toward plugins that can package reusable instructions, reference material, and connections to outside services.

Under OpenAI's plugin architecture, a plugin can include one or more skills containing instructions and resources for repeatable workflows, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposing tools and external systems, or both. ChatGPT and Codex share a universal plugin directory, although some capabilities can remain specific to a particular environment.

For organizations, that makes the change more than a simple renaming exercise. A company could package recurring workflows into skills while using MCP servers or connected apps to give those workflows access to enterprise systems and data.

OpenAI says creators will be able to migrate an existing GPT through the My GPTs interface. The GPT's instructions become a skill in the replacement plugin, while knowledge files are copied into plugin reference files and connected apps can be carried over.

Not everything transfers automatically. Existing GPT conversations do not migrate, the selected model does not carry over, and Custom Actions may have to be rebuilt using an available app or a custom MCP server.

Sharing also changes. Migrated plugins start private, existing GPT users do not automatically receive access to the replacement, and prior sharing settings do not carry over.

OpenAI is also cautioning organizations against assuming that migration will preserve behavior exactly. "A migrated plugin may respond differently," the company says, recommending that users retest familiar prompts, reference-material use, required output formats, and integrations before relying on the replacement.

That warning has contributed to pushback from some GPT builders, who argue that plugins do not fully reproduce the dedicated and predictable environment of a Custom GPT. Other complaints have focused on sharing, migration complexity, and differences in how migrated workflows use instructions and reference material.

Despite those concerns, OpenAI is clearly consolidating around plugins as its common mechanism for extending its AI products. Its developer documentation now describes plugins as packages users can "discover, install, share, and publish" across ChatGPT and Codex, replacing the separate-custom-assistant model with reusable AI capabilities that can be combined with enterprise tools and services.

For more information, go to the OpenAI site.

David Ramel is an editor and writer at Converge 360.

#49. Harvard logs $100M surplus despite 20% drop in federal research money

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A cost-cutting effort and spike in endowment money helped the Ivy League institution weather political and economic instability in fiscal 2026.

University leaders invoked Harvard’s resilience in letters introducing the university’s latest financial report.

“Our stewardship has been focused on driving efficiencies and adapting our operations to meet the uncertainty of the moment,” Meredith Weenick, Harvard’s executive vice president, said in a statement Thursday. “Our focus has been on resiliency.”

However, resiliency came at a cost, namely a reduction to the university’s employee headcount that included layoffs. “Those two facts — a surplus, and a smaller community — sit uneasily together,” Kalra and Barakett wrote. “Yet they cannot be separated.”

Also key to Harvard’s resiliency is its massive endowment, which is typically the largest of any U.S. institution by billions of dollars. By the end of the fiscal 2026 year in late June, Harvard’s endowment was valued at $68 billion, up over 19% from last year.

Investment income grew 5.1% year over year to $2.9 billion. Those earnings include the $2.6 billion the university withdrew from its endowment, amounting to 39% of its operating revenue in fiscal 2026.

That kind of money helped Harvard plug the research funding shortfall amid the Trump administration's ongoing political attacks on the university.

“Fewer new awards and slower spending on existing awards drove the decline — the consequence of a longstanding relationship between the federal government and American research universities now called into question,” Kalra and Barakett wrote.

Amid the decline, Harvard put up $400 million of its own money toward the $1.2 billion it logged in research activity, or about one-third of the total.

Kalra said in a statement Thursday that the university was working with foundations and industry to diversify its research funding going forward.

#51. How to choose between two job offers: 6 tips

Glassdoor Team | Author & Career Expert at Glassdoor | Sep 30, 2026

Job offer decline rates fell to 21.4% for interviews that began between January 1 and April 15, 2026, according to Glassdoor Economic Research¹. That's down 5.1 percentage points year-over-year.

Daniel Zhao, Glassdoor's chief economist, says workers are "favoring taking any job over holding out for the best job."

If you're in the fortunate position of choosing between two offers, compare how each fits your long-term goals, total pay, culture, manager, and daily routine, then check the result against your gut. Here are six tips to help you choose between two job offers.

When you're interviewing for a job, you sell yourself. Once you have two job offers, consider what each company can do for you.

Review what you learned about the job, organization, and culture during interviews. Then, ask yourself:

Choosing gets hard when the job you want less pays more. But if you're bored 40 or more hours per week, a higher salary won't do much for your happiness.

Still, pay shapes satisfaction. Glassdoor research found that 71% of well-compensated workers gave their employer a 4- or 5-star overall rating. That's more than 10 percentage points higher than under-compensated workers².

Compare base pay, bonus, and benefits on Glassdoor Salaries, then negotiate your salary. If your preferred job pays less, ask whether it can match. An attorney on Glassdoor Community put it plainly: "You can honestly say look I'm deciding here and have another offer that's 6% more."

If one position's pay can't support you, go with the other one. If both meet your needs, choose the job that fits your values.

Cultural fit isn't a one-way street. A toxic workplace drains you, while a culture that values and challenges you builds passion.

Ask your interviewer, reach out to current employees, or investigate employee reviews online. As a CEO-Founder on Glassdoor Community advised, "Some warning signs I'd pay attention to are high employee turnover, the same complaints appearing repeatedly in reviews."

Check for other red flags to spot before taking the job. Then, decide which culture you want: collaboration, independence, flexibility, or new challenges.

Your manager shapes your daily experience. One director on Glassdoor Community summed it up: "Your boss will make or break your experience!"

A bad manager could make you lose motivation or even want to quit, Jerry Maguire-style. A good manager motivates you and acts as a mentor, so assess each one before you accept.

Ask how they onboard new hires and how many direct reports have been promoted or stayed. Talk to current employees, and learn what separates good and bad managers.

If you're wondering how to decide between two jobs, the decision isn't clear-cut. List a typical day in each role, and ask yourself these questions:

Put both offers in one chart, and rank your priorities. Ask the employer to fill any blanks. If the jobs are otherwise similar, a shorter commute can break the tie.

Finally, check in with your inner voice. Ask yourself:

You know your work preferences better than friends or family do. A principal materials engineer on Glassdoor Community trusted a gut read: "I walked away from an offer because I could immediately tell the hiring manager would have been a nightmare to work with."

Sometimes, you have to take a risk and leap into the job that excites you.

If neither offer fits, keep looking. Upload your resume to find a job match that fits.

Can I ask for more time to decide between two job offers?

Yes. Thank the employer, name a date you'll respond by, and ask the other employer about its timeline.

How do I turn down the offer I don't take?

Respond promptly, thank the recruiter, and give a brief, gracious reason without criticizing the company.

¹ Glassdoor Worklife Trends 2026: Midyear Check-in, Glassdoor Economic Research, June 24, 2026. Job offer refusal rates across 180,179 Glassdoor interview reviews, for interviews that began between January 2020 and April 15, 2026 and resulted in an offer. A margin of error was not reported by the source.

² Conversation starter: Does money buy loyalty?, Katherine Engelman, Glassdoor data scientist, June 22, 2026. Reviews from 2024–2025. Users were classified by comparing self-reported salary (January 2018–March 2026) with Glassdoor's predicted median pay for their title, location, employer, sector, and experience.

More than 15% above meant well-compensated; more than 15% below meant under-compensated. Only users with an approved review within two years of their salary report were included. A sample size and margin of error were not reported by the source.

#56. Proving academic ROI can be tough, but this Delaware district has a plan

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A Christina School District leader shares at the annual ASBO conference how the district developed a tool to explore if its programs were improving student outcomes.

PITTSBURGH — As school districts work to improve lagging student outcomes, there’s very limited information on whether those investments are proving successful, experts say.

“As a result, sometimes budget decisions are based on our best guesses about what's working in our system, the loudest voices in the room, or compliance with specific funding requirements, but not necessarily what we know about the impact on student performance,” said Kelsey Krausen, director of education finance at WestEd.

Delaware’s Christina School District has partnered with WestEd to develop a way to measure student outcomes from specific district programs and initiatives.

Krausen and Nathalie Princilus, supervisor of grants and unique programs at the 13,000-student district, discussed how to implement such a practice and tool to ensure academic return on investments during a Thursday session at the Association of School Business Officials International’s 2026 Annual Conference & Expo in Pittsburgh.

Christina School District worked with WestEd to develop an academic ROI dashboard that allows district leaders to consistently evaluate student performance from programmatic investments. The dashboard, which launched in July, can show the cost of a program alongside data measuring students’ academic outcomes from those programs, Princilus said.

The dashboard can also compare different programs and their outcomes, and it includes a reflection section for leaders to answer why a program did or didn’t work.

Before Christina School District engaged in its academic ROI evaluation, about half of the district’s programming had no clear methods to measure student outcomes, Princilus said. Measuring ROI is especially important for the district as it experiences enrollment shifts and financial instability following pandemic-era investments, she said. The number of students attending Christina School District has fallen from 13,553 in fall 2022 to 12,799 in fall 2026 — a 5.6% drop.

During the surge of federal COVID-19 recovery funds, Princilus said, the district invested a lot of its dollars into staffing. Christina School District has also made significant investments in programs across multiple funding streams as student needs and operational costs both continue to increase.

While Christina School District had access to ample data to measure student outcomes from all of its investments, Princilus said, the district still needed a data measurement system that was consistently implemented across all of its schools.

That would require more ownership and fidelity in data entry districtwide to help better track student outcomes, because otherwise the goals of certain programs would be difficult to measure, she said.

Prior to the dashboard, one way the district began to measure academic ROI was by examining its in-school suspension program, which is an unfunded, state-mandated initiative meant to reduce out-of-school suspensions. Princilus said the district has spent $1 million in contracts to facilitate the program, which requires a tiered intervention support system for students.

Although the Christina School District has used this strategy for the past four years, ultimately, the district realized that its implementation of the in-school suspension program didn’t have a strong academic ROI, Princilus said. The district discovered this after digging into questions about the rate of student recidivism among participants, data on academic and behavioral interventions, students’ GPAs and attendance rates over time, and student demographic data.

“So we have been spending, for some time, a huge portion of some grant budget on a strategy that's mandated. However, we did not do the authentic work of ensuring that the implementation and the program evaluation” were underway, Princilus said.

This process helped the district understand and communicate to its school leaders that there needs to be stronger and more consistent implementation strategies for its in-school suspension program, she said.

Now, the academic ROI dashboard is a useful tool for Christina School District leaders to communicate with their superintendent, school board or local taxpayers about why a program may need to sunset or change in its implementation, Princilus said.

Krausen said the goal of academic ROI analysis is to “help our leaders within the system define a set of small priorities, understand the programs and services that are supporting those priorities with defined outcomes, and be able to measure their impact on students, on specific student groups over time, and ultimately lead to better outcomes for students.”

Sometimes, it can be difficult to cut programs that are not showing promising results for students, because some educators are attached to certain initiatives, Princilus said.

Even when school leaders face pushback on proposed cuts because of that emotional attachment to some programs, Princilus said she encourages school leaders to keep focusing on student outcomes and ensuring investments match that.

#57. Trump admin reignites court battle over student deportations based on speech

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The federal government appealed a court decision that ruled its efforts to revoke student visas based on protected speech were unconstitutional.

The DHS did not immediately respond to questions Thursday. It appealed the case to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

The lawsuit over the Trump administration's actions dates back to August 2025, when Stanford University’s independent student newspaper alleged the federal government sought to deport students that it deemed to hold “anti-American or anti-Israel” views.

The administration's actions created a “pall of fear” that is “incompatible with American liberty," the newspaper alleged in its lawsuit. The complaint cited decisions by Stanford’s international students to turn down stories, ask that their previous articles be taken down or quit the publication entirely out of fear that their legal status would be threatened.

This summer, U.S. District Judge Noël Wise sided with the plaintiffs and said that the Trump administration has targeted people over speech it disfavored on other topics as well, such as criticisms of right-wing commentator Charlie Kirk after he was fatally shot at Utah Valley University.

“Tomorrow, or perhaps even today, targets may include anyone in the United States who exercises their freedom of speech to simply express opinions the government does not like,” she wrote in her decision. “This downward spiral is antithetical to our Constitution that recognizes our right to speak freely.”

A recent research paper found a strong correlation between pro-Palestinian campus protests in spring 2024 and the federal government terminating the legal status of international students at those colleges.

The findings offer "compelling evidence that immigration authorities were targeting political expression on U.S. campuses for punitive enforcement," according to the paper.

#59. AI Leaders Warn of Risks at United Nations Security Council Briefing

The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face recently joined AI researcher Yoshua Bengio at the United Nations headquarters in New York on September 23 to warn the UN Security Council about the security risks of increasingly capable AI.

They did not offer a single plan for managing those risks. Bengio called for licensing and independent safety reviews. OpenAI's Sam Altman proposed common standards that countries could adopt through their own laws. Anthropic's Dario Amodei urged AI developers to slow down when safety work cannot keep pace. Hugging Face's Clément Delangue warned that limiting access to capable systems could leave defenders at a disadvantage.

France, which held the Security Council's rotating presidency, convened the meeting on AI and international security. The discussion exposed a difficult question for governments: how to oversee technology that crosses borders when countries disagree about who should set the rules.

Bengio, co-chair of the UN's Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, challenged the idea that competition forces companies to keep building more powerful systems. "The race is not a law of nature: it is the product of choices," he said in his published remarks. "They've told us they would slow down if they could. They can."

He called on developers to show independent experts that frontier systems are safe to train and deploy. He also proposed incident reporting, licensing, and liability insurance. Bengio identified catastrophic misuse, concentrated power, and the loss of human control as risks that require international cooperation.

Altman acknowledged the danger of moving too quickly. "We have unilaterally slowed down in the past. We will do so in the future," he said, according to remarks published by OpenAI. Decisions about AI's direction "cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," he added.

Altman proposed complementary national and international standards to measure frontier AI capabilities, assess risks, and test safeguards. He said countries should be able to compare evidence and verify commitments. He also called for faster reporting of serious incidents and secure channels for sharing emerging threats. Such standards should accommodate both open and closed models without favoring established companies, he said.

Amodei made a more direct commitment about the pace of Anthropic's releases: "We will slow down as much as necessary," he told the council. He identified two principal concerns: the misuse of AI to develop biological weapons and the possibility that advanced systems could outstrip developers' ability to control them.

The Anthropic chief proposed placing outside evaluators inside AI companies with access comparable to employees. He suggested that governments begin with a narrow agreement against using AI to make biological weapons, then develop ways to evaluate models and verify commitments across borders. He also called for common testing standards and a system for notifying other countries of significant AI incidents.

Delangue drew on a July incident in which Hugging Face disclosed an AI agent cyberattack. He called for stronger monitoring and disclosure, but argued that safety also depends on giving defenders access to capable tools. The central danger, he said, was "asymmetry of powerful AI" between attackers and defenders, large companies and everyone else, and wealthy countries and the rest of the world. His team used an open-source model while responding to the attack, he said.

The U.S. government opposed a broader international regulatory role. White House science adviser Michael Kratsios told the council that countries should develop their own ability to use and govern the technology. In the U.S. statement, he rejected new global governance structures and used the phrase "superintelligence, formerly known as AI," adopting President Donald Trump's terminology from his General Assembly speech the previous day.

The four AI briefers differed on how far oversight should go and how widely capable systems should be available. They agreed on a narrower point: Governments need better ways to understand what advanced AI systems can do and to detect when safeguards fail.

#61. 3 ways to see if you’re getting paid what you’re worth

Senior Manager of Content Strategy & Optimization | Sep 30, 2026

How much (or how little) you're getting paid can often shape how you feel about your job. In a June 2026 Glassdoor Economic Research analysis, 71% of well-compensated workers gave their employer a 4- or 5-star rating.¹ That’s more than 10 percentage points higher than under-compensated workers.

Knowing whether you’re being paid fairly is critical information when negotiating your salary and benefits, whether at your current job or a prospective one.

Here are a couple of laws regarding equal pay that are worth knowing:

1. The Equal Pay Act requires that men and women in the same workplace be given equal pay for equal work. Other laws, including Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, ban pay discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, age, or disability.

2. Pay transparency laws are making salary ranges easier to find. As of December 2024, 14 state laws and seven local laws required some pay transparency, according to the Society for Human Resource Management (SHRM). Now job seekers can know what to expect at the start of the interview process and avoid the salary negotiation dance later on.

Here are three ways to check whether you’re being paid fairly.

Thanks to pay transparency laws, you can ask a company about its salary range for a job or find it on the listing itself. Then, see if it lines up with employees’ actual experiences.

Sometimes the simplest way to get answers is to ask around. Asking teammates about their salaries can feel awkward.

If you’re comfortable asking, and they’re open to telling you, that’s great. You’ll also want more data than a few coworkers can give you, gathered more discreetly.

The Salary & Compensation bowl on Glassdoor Community is a place to get candid answers and advice from workers about pay. It gives you the insider view when you’re fielding a new job offer and wondering whether it’s high or low. It also shows you which benefits and support to ask for.

When chatbots and recruiters give you different numbers, real figures from peers settle the question. A Managing Director on Glassdoor Community offered this advice: "If you can't find info online, I would ask people in the industry. It never hurts to reach out and inquire so you have some real numbers."

Another way to learn about a company’s treatment and compensation of employees is to look up company reviews on Glassdoor and Indeed profiles. Current and past employees review companies on factors like:

Reviews and salary reports also show average pay for individual roles and how satisfied employees are with it.

You can also compare two companies side by side to see how they stack up. You can explore how your skills are valued across different sectors, which shows you what you could earn if you move into another industry.

Before any salary negotiation, check the going rate for someone with your skills and level of experience.

Salary tools like Glassdoor Salaries show how much people earn in a given role based on factors such as location and years of experience. They also give you a better sense of your total pay. That’s how much you’d earn from base salary plus additional pay like annual or performance-based bonuses.

That analysis used a 15% gap as the dividing line. Workers earning at least 15% less than expected for their job title, location, employer, and years of experience counted as under-compensated.¹ Katherine Engelman, a data scientist at Glassdoor, wrote that the analysis shows "money can buy happier employees."

"Comparing my salary with similar experience/titles on Glassdoor, I’m sitting at about average so I’m fairly happy with my salary." That’s how one Design Engineer summed up their own benchmarking on Glassdoor Community.

If the numbers show a gap, take them to your manager. One manager on Glassdoor Community suggests "asking if your company has a process for salary market adjustments."

Then explain that your research shows your pay is below company and industry standards. Learn how to know if you’re underpaid, then use your data to negotiate your salary.

Is it legal to talk about pay with your coworkers?

Yes, for most private-sector employees. The National Labor Relations Board (NLRB) says federal law protects your right to discuss wages with coworkers, and policies banning those conversations are unlawful.

Can you look up what a specific person earns?

Not on Glassdoor. Glassdoor Salaries shows anonymous, self-reported pay grouped by job title, company, and location, so you can benchmark your role without seeing anyone’s paycheck.

¹ Glassdoor Economic Research, "Conversation starter: Does money buy loyalty?" by Katherine Engelman, data scientist, published June 22, 2026. The analysis compared a sample of Glassdoor users’ self-reported salaries, submitted January 2018–March 2026, with Glassdoor’s estimated median salary. That estimate reflects each user’s job title, location, employer, employer’s sector, and years of experience.

Users more than 15% above the estimate were classed as well-compensated and those more than 15% below as under-compensated. Only users who left an approved Glassdoor review within two years of submitting pay were included. Ratings reflect reviews from 2024 and 2025.

The source does not report a sample size or margin of error.

Want to compare notes with people in your field? Join the Glassdoor Community.

Stacia Doss, senior manager of content strategy and optimization, has been with Glassdoor since 2022, where she oversees content strategy for job seekers. She brings more than a decade of editorial expertise spanning healthcare, tech, and Fortune 10 companies. Stacia holds a bachelor's degree in web journalism from the University of Memphis and a Master of Arts degree in PR and Advertising from DePaul University.

#64. Redesigned Microsoft Copilot Will Build Apps and Work on Its Own

Micorosft has announced that it's redesigning Copilot, the company's all-encompassing AI assistant, so users can hand off complex tasks, build tools by describing what they need, and assign work to an agent that keeps going after they log off.

The new Copilot experience has three main parts: Home, Code, and Autopilot. It also brings Word, Excel, and PowerPoint into the Copilot app. For users, the pitch is simple: Start a task in one place and stay there as it grows from a quick question into a document, an app, or a longer-running project. Most of the new capabilities are still rolling out or in preview.

Home puts Chat and Copilot Cowork together. Chat remains the place for quick answers, research, and drafts. Cowork handles work a user wants to delegate, such as preparing a briefing or pulling together a response to a request for proposals. Microsoft said Copilot eventually will route requests to Chat, Cowork, or Code on its own.

Office in Copilot will allow users to create a Word document, Excel workbook, or PowerPoint deck without leaving that experience. The files remain editable in the regular Office apps, and colleagues can work on them at the same time. Someone building a presentation, for example, could draw on a workbook, draft the slides, and keep refining both files from within Copilot.

Code is aimed at people who need a tool but might never open a development environment. A user can describe a tracker, dashboard, app, or workflow in plain language and have Copilot build it. Microsoft calls these "small, purpose-built solutions." The feature uses the same underlying technology as GitHub Copilot and runs in a sandboxed environment. A separate Copilot Managed Runtime, now in preview, lets organizations host and share the resulting apps within Microsoft 365.

Then there is Autopilot, previously known as Scout. It is designed for work that does not end with a single response: following a discussion, checking in with stakeholders, or keeping a project moving over several days. "Give it a name, a role, and a goal," Microsoft said. Autopilot runs in the cloud and has its own identity, memory, and workspace in the customer's tenant. Microsoft said its actions are subject to permissions, auditing, and organizational controls.

Those longer-running tasks also change how customers pay for Copilot. In a separate pricing post, Microsoft said everyday work in Chat and Microsoft 365 apps will remain covered by a per-user subscription. Cowork, Code, and Autopilot will be billed separately through usage-based Copilot Credits. A Copilot user subscription will still be needed to access those features.

For enterprise customers, the features that charge by usage will stay off until an admin sets up a spending policy in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Microsoft said there will be no charges before then. Admins can set budgets for the whole organization or for specific groups, limit how much individual users can spend, and get alerts when costs approach a set amount. Reports will show who is using the features and which tasks are driving costs.

Microsoft is bringing Code and Copilot Managed Runtime under those cost controls alongside Cowork. Copilot Studio agents are expected to follow in October. Before turning the features on for more employees, IT departments will need to decide who can use them, how much they can spend and which tasks are worth the extra cost.

Home and Code will begin rolling out through Microsoft's Frontier early access program in the coming weeks. Code's Frontier rollout starts at the end of September, when Autopilot also expands to private preview.

For more information, visit the Microsoft site.

Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

#65. Judge declines to block Trump’s March anti-DEI order for federal contractors

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The ruling rejected plaintiffs’ constitutional arguments but said that the directive only pertains to conduct that is “already prohibited by federal law.”

In their lawsuit, plaintiffs argued that Trump’s March order was overly broad and vague and violated their First and Fifth Amendment rights.

“The Administration views discussion of race and ethnicity as unlawful, and the very concepts of diversity, equity, and inclusion as discriminatory. But that is flat wrong,” they argued in their original complaint. “The Contractors Order sanctions legal, and laudable, expression on race or ethnicity, and in doing so, violates the free speech, free association, and due process rights of Plaintiffs and their members.”

The plaintiffs include the National Association of Diversity Officers in Higher Education, the American Association of University Professors, and United Academics of Maryland-University of Maryland, College Park.

Abelson, a Biden appointee, disagreed with the groups’ constitutional arguments.

He pointed to the order’s “operative phrase” that banned “disparate treatment based on race or ethnicity,” terminology that the judge noted was synonymous with intentional discrimination. That language “has a settled antidiscrimination-law meaning that materially narrows the provision’s reach,” Abelson wrote.

Democracy Forward, the advocacy nonprofit representing the plaintiffs, said the ruling provides “clarity” for federal contractors and “defangs” Trump’s order.

In a news release Wednesday, the group pointed to language from Abelson explaining that the order “only prohibits contractors from engaging in conduct that is already prohibited by federal law: intentional discrimination on the basis of race or ethnicity.”

In an emailed statement Thursday, NADOHE President and CEO Emelyn dela Peña said, “The ruling was a clear win for NADOHE and our members, both substantively and in terms of the ruling’s practical impact, despite the court denying our request for a preliminary injunction.”

She added, “As a result of this ruling, leaders of colleges and universities no longer need to second-guess whether their lawful activities to support inclusive and diverse campus communities violate the executive order.”

In his opinion, Abelson cited in part precedent from an appeals court ruling against some of the same plaintiffs suing over earlier Trump executive orders targeting DEI.

One of those orders directed federal agencies to cancel “equity-related” grants and contracts to “to the maximum extent allowed by law,” while another required federal funding recipients to certify that they do not engage in activities “that violate any applicable Federal anti-discrimination laws.”

After a lower court initially blocked the orders, the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals concluded that the certification requirement only required recipients to affirm that their DEI programs don’t violate antidiscrimination law.

Moreover, the groups could still challenge specific enforcement actions stemming from that order that they believe misinterpret antidiscrimination law, a majority for the appeals panel wrote.

#66. Ohio school choice program ‘undermining’ public schools, state court rules

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A three-judge panel unanimously found a voucher program’s expansion violates a state requirement for a “thorough and efficient” school system.

The lawsuit, Columbus City School District, et al. v. State of Ohio, was filed by a coalition of school districts in 2022.

"The EdChoice Scholarship Program poses an existential threat to Ohio’s public school system," the coalition stated in their original complaint. "Not only does this voucher program unconstitutionally usurp Ohio’s public tax dollars to subsidize private school tuitions, it does so by depleting Ohio’s foundation funding — the pool of money out of which the state funds Ohio’s public schools — otherwise available to already struggling school districts for the education of their students."

The 10th District Court panel, which examined fiscal data, agreed in its Thursday decision. Had the state EdChoice program not been funded in fiscal years 2023 and 2024, the state's public school funding plan could have been fully funded, the judges said.

In fiscal years 2023 and 2024, public schools received only 50% and 66% of the Fair School Funding Plan, a bipartisan multiyear state funding plan, respectively.

Overall, in fiscal year 2024, public schools received only $7.1 billion compared to the $7.8 billion they would have received if fully funded — a difference of approximately the same amount used to fund the school choice program, the judges said.

In fiscal years 2024 and 2025, the school choice program cost taxpayers almost $1.4 billion, according to the opinion.

Judges clarified, however, that not all forms of school vouchers violate the state's constitution, and their decision is limited to how the state's EdChoice and related programs are currently structured and funded.

The scathing decision comes as the U.S. is set to launch its first nationwide federal school choice program, which provides taxpayers a credit if they donate to scholarship-granting organizations that distribute funds for families to use on expenses for public and private — including religious — schools.

Ohio has opted into that program, which begins in 2027.

The controversial federal program is expected to provide an estimated $26 billion in taxpayer contributions annually for education expenses.

#68. 6 red flags to spot before taking the job

Program Manager of Corporate Marketing | Sep 29, 2026

Glassdoor reviewers were 6.7 times as likely to mention a toxic boss or toxic management in 2025 as in 2018.¹ Assume you'll spot even more once you're inside, so look harder during hiring for the signs of a toxic workplace before you accept.

You can rarely tell how a company truly operates until you're on the inside. Still, read the signals during the hiring process, and lean on people who have been there. Glassdoor Community members and Gorick Ng, a Harvard career adviser and author of The Unspoken Rules, shared the red flags they watch for.

Look for signs of a toxic workplace before your first day. Watch for these six red flags, flagged by Glassdoor Community members and career adviser Gorick Ng.

Gorick Ng calls high turnover the most important red flag. It means, he says, "it doesn't seem like anyone's been able to stay at this organization for more than a year." A revolving door points to problems with pay, leadership, culture, or workload. Companies rarely advertise it, so dig a little:

Low turnover, by contrast, is a green flag. One Project Manager on Glassdoor Community put it simply: "Crazy turnover, voluntary and involuntary."

Treat any "family" framing as a cue to test the company's boundaries and support, not as a warm perk. Loyalty talk often blurs professional lines and shows up as:

The word itself isn't the problem; the pressure behind it is. One Business Data Consultant on Glassdoor Community warned against it. "Just preaching we're a family is a red flag … they will replace and forget about you before your body is cold."

Be wary of "we work long hours, not because we have to, but because we love what we do." A good employer won't use your passion to keep you on the clock, so don't sign up to be an octo-hire. One Engineer on Glassdoor Community put it plainly. "If they … mention people will 'wear many hats,' those are bad signs … the business model could be centered on burning people out."

Negotiating pay is part of hiring, so a company that dodges it is telling you something. Be cautious of a "competitive salary" or "generous benefits" with no specifics. One Project Manager on Glassdoor Community said, "Vague answers about workload, defensiveness around pay, and inconsistent stories between interviewers always worry me."

Notice what an interviewer asks, because the questions can be the flag. One Administrative Assistant on Glassdoor Community flagged a telling prompt: "asking if I had any experience in handling … a temperamental coworker or superior." That kind of screen hints at deeper problems.

Slow down if an offer comes before you finish interviewing, or if you can't sleep on it. A Case Manager on Glassdoor Community flagged one version: "they say you can start that day or next day." A healthy employer gives you room to decide.

Don't write off a company over one bad interview, but don't ignore it either. Comb through reviews, ask your network, and learn which interview questions reveal a toxic boss. List what you want from the role, then weigh each priority against the flags; a job with good managers can still be a launchpad.

Time your due diligence well. Glassdoor's Economic Research team found workers are 5.7 times as likely to mention toxic management after leaving a job as while still in it.¹ So vet hard before you accept.

If you're already inside a toxic job, act early. Set boundaries with your manager, escalate to human resources (HR) if it persists, and know that moving on is valid. Before you accept your next role, upload your resume to find your tailored job match.

What should you do if you spot red flags after you've already accepted? Document specific incidents, set clear boundaries early, and keep your network and job search warm so you can move if things don't improve.

How can you tell whether a company's culture claims are real? Cross-check what recruiters say against recent Glassdoor reviews, and ask current employees for concrete examples; claims no one can back up are the warning.

Is a fast job offer always a red flag? Not always. A small, decisive team can move quickly, but pressure to sign before you've reviewed the details is the real problem.

¹ Source: Glassdoor Economic Research, "Conversation starter: Is toxic management spreading?" by Chris Martin, senior economist, May 1, 2026. It reflects a pool of 9.6 million Glassdoor reviews. The analysis uses 2018 as the baseline and covers reviews left from 2021 to 2025. Because it is a full-population review-text analysis rather than a sample-based poll, no margin of error applies.

Autumn Williams, program manager of Corporate Marketing, has been with Glassdoor since 2025, where she leads and supports content strategy and editorial planning across various teams and initiatives, including Glassdoor Community. She brings seven years of marketing expertise spanning the gaming, fintech, and advertising industries. Autumn holds a bachelor's degree in Communications from Appalachian State University.

#71. AI Platform Behind 12,000 E-mail Breaches Dismantled

The platform moved quickly. Since launching in February, EvilTokens had been tied to more than 12,000 compromised inboxes across over 10,000 organizations worldwide, according to Microsoft. Its victims included businesses and institutions in financial services, healthcare, construction, real estate, wholesale distribution, and higher education.

Microsoft and its partners seized 50 websites used to operate EvilTokens and disabled more than 150 additional domains supporting the service. The Metropolitan Police Service in the United Kingdom also arrested two men on Sept. 11 in connection with the alleged operation.

At the center of EvilTokens was an AI chatbot designed specifically for cybercrime. Once attackers gained access to an inbox, the chatbot could analyze messages, map relationships, identify employees involved in payments, and recommend ways to impersonate trusted contacts.

Microsoft said the platform helped criminals determine "who to target, who to impersonate," and how to get the most money from a compromised organization.

Business e-mail compromise has traditionally required attackers to manually comb through messages, learn how an organization handles payments, and find the right person to impersonate. However, EvilTokens simplified the entire process by automating much of that work.

The tools could quickly sort through a stolen inbox, summarize or translate messages, find invoices and wire-transfer discussions, and identify the people who moved money. EvilTokens could then draft messages that sounded like they came from the victim. It packaged all of this with mailbox access, phishing tools, management dashboards, and even customer support.

The service was sold through Telegram for a $1,500 startup fee, followed by a $500 monthly subscription. Microsoft's complaint also described a bulk e-mail tool that cost $600 a month and a more advanced e-mail delivery platform priced at $1,000 a month.

To break into a target, EvilTokens relied on device-code phishing. Victims were sent to a real Microsoft sign-in page and persuaded to enter an authentication code. The login process looked legitimate because it was, but the code quietly authorized a session controlled by the attacker.

That also made cleanup more complicated. The attackers stole OAuth tokens and authenticated sessions instead of passwords, so a password reset alone might not remove their access. Administrators also needed to revoke the stolen tokens and active sessions.

According to Microsoft's complaint,  EvilTokens used fake Microsoft 365 security notices and other branded templates to direct users into the device authentication flow. Once inside, attackers could use Microsoft Graph and other APIs to search and monitor a mailbox.

The company also found that AI played a role in creating EvilTokens itself. Investigators said much of the platform appeared to have been "vibe coded," with its developers using AI to quickly build and expand the service. EvilTokens reportedly drew on multiple AI models, including improperly integrated services from Groq and OpenAI.

Microsoft and Health-ISAC filed a civil lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia against Felix Utomi, Waidi Segun Adams, and five unnamed defendants. The complaint alleges violations of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, Electronic Communications Privacy Act, Lanham Act and federal racketeering law.

The court authorized Microsoft to take control of or disable domains connected to the operation. Microsoft worked with Cloudflare, Coinbase, OpenAI, Railway, SpyCloud, the Shadowserver Foundation, and TRM Labs on the disruption. Health-ISAC joined the case because healthcare organizations were among the targets.

This marks the Microsoft Digital Crimes Unit's 40th court-authorized disruption and its first targeting an end-to-end, AI-enabled cybercrime service.

EvilTokens' infrastructure may be offline, but the model behind it is unlikely to disappear. The operation showed how AI can turn a stolen inbox into an immediately useful fraud playbook, allowing less-experienced criminals to launch attacks that once required considerable time and skill.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.

Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

#74. Democratic lawmakers accuse Education Department of ‘frontloading’ grants

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

A letter from two key Senate Appropriations Committee members says the agency’s approach is making it easier to cancel funding in future years.

Democratic lawmakers on Tuesday accused the U.S. Department of Education of "frontloading" grants — or making multiyear funding available in one lump sum ahead of time rather than funding a larger number of grants over time, as is typical.

This approach has led to the withholding of approximately $630 million in appropriated resources across approximately 35 grant programs, according to a letter sent to U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon by lawmakers from the Senate Appropriations Committee.

"In implementing this policy, the Department is intentionally and sharply limiting the number of new grants it will award, by concentrating funds into fewer grants and withholding significant portions of appropriated resources for use in future budget periods," said U.S. Senators Patty Murray, D-Wash., and Tammy Baldwin, D-Wisc, in the Oct. 13 letter.

Murray is vice chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations, and Baldwin is a ranking member of the Appropriations Subcommittee on Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies.

If the Education Department had stuck with its traditional approach of funding on an annual basis, the agency could have awarded more than 1,000 grants this year across areas including evidence-based student literacy programs, student mental health supports, education research, and recruiting and preparing teachers, the lawmakers said.

In one example cited, the lawmakers said the department frontloaded grants in the Innovative Approaches to Literacy program. Though the agency announced it would make up to 35 awards using the $30 million in funds earmarked in the fiscal year 2026 appropriations law, it issued only four new awards and set aside $13 million for future years for those grants, Baldwin and Murray said.

“The better question is why would an Administration dedicated to improving literacy outcomes and supporting child care for low-income student parents continue the failed approach of previous Administrations?” said Ellen Keast, communications director for the undersecretary at the Education Department, in an Oct. 14 email to K-12 Dive. “Yes, we are returning education to the states and have furthered that effort by funding the highest-quality grantees that will help kids learn to read and support parents in college.”

However, Baldwin and Murray said the Education Department's new funding approach runs counter to Congressional directives and claimed the department had adopted it to further a goal of eliminating the department and some programs.

The lawmakers' concern over the department's changed funding distribution method comes amid ongoing turbulence over the Trump administration's grant funding cancellations. Many such decisions have been tied to grant recipients' use of diversity, equity and inclusion practices. Multiple lawsuits have stemmed from those cancellations, with judges sometimes ruling them unlawful and requiring the department to backpedal even after the department had already issued new grant funding priorities and awards.

It also comes as the Education Department is trying to codify its controversial approach to terminating grant funding even after those approaches landed the agency in legal hot water. In August, the department proposed a rule that would give itself broad authority to end grants, including "for convenience."

Under the changes, the department could abruptly terminate, discontinue or withhold discretionary funding based on a retroactive review of applications — and whether those applications align with an administration’s changing policies.

If this and other proposed changes from the government go through, Baldwin and Murray said in their Oct. 13 letter, "this means the Department could easily terminate all these frontloaded funds, effectively terminating a large swath of FY2026 funds that Congress appropriated on a bipartisan basis."

#77. New Industry Alliance to Work Toward Common Security Model for AI Agents

Okta has announced a coalition bringing together major cloud, security, data and application vendors to create a shared architecture for securing AI agents across enterprise environments.

The 12 founding members of the new Blueprint Alliance are AWS, CrowdStrike, Databricks, Docker, Google Cloud, Lovable, Okta, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, Wiz and Zscaler. GE Appliances and World Central Kitchen are participating as strategic advisors.

The effort expands an earlier Okta framework into an open, multi-vendor reference architecture intended to address a basic problem with enterprise AI agents: An agent can be created in one system, authenticated through another, access tools and data from several others, and be monitored by yet another security platform.

The Alliance is focused less on how agents are built and more on how organizations can govern them consistently across vendor boundaries.

The Blueprint Alliance architecture organizes agent security around four questions: Where are my agents? What can they do? What are they doing? How do I respond?

Those questions translate into several practical areas:

The reference architecture also covers development-related systems. Its whitepaper includes agent frameworks, code repositories, CI/CD environments, code assistants, tool registries, Model Context Protocol servers, and command-line tools among the components that may need to be discovered or governed.

That makes the initiative relevant to development teams deploying agents that interact with internal APIs, MCP tools, databases, SaaS applications, or other agents. The architecture calls for those connections and permissions to remain visible and controllable as agents move from development into production.

A major part of the Alliance's work will be testing how security information and controls can move between products from different vendors.

The initial architecture references several existing standards and protocols, including MCP for agent-to-tool interactions, the Open Cybersecurity Schema Framework for security telemetry, and the Shared Signals Framework and Continuous Access Evaluation Profile for exchanging risk information.

The goal is for one part of an enterprise stack to be able to detect a risk condition and pass that information to another control point that can act on it. Depending on the implementation, that could include revoking access or containing an agent whose behavior has changed.

The Alliance says members will build and test reference integrations and publish results as interoperability work progresses. Specific cross-vendor implementations and performance results were not documented in the launch announcement.

Founding member Lovable also published a developer-oriented explanation of its participation, describing organizations that may have internally built agents, agents imported through SaaS platforms and locally running agents that all need to be inventoried and governed under a common model.

The Alliance's whitepaper recommends that organizations begin with foundational capabilities such as unified logging, telemetry, and agent discovery rather than attempting to deploy every control at once.

The architecture is available for community use, and the Alliance says it will continue evolving as members test integrations and additional participants become involved. Timelines for individual vendor integrations have not been published.

For more information, check out the Okta announcement here.

David Ramel is an editor and writer at Converge 360.

#78. 6 things to avoid saying when negotiating your salary

Glassdoor Team | Author & Career Expert at Glassdoor | Sep 28, 2026

According to a LendingTree survey, 82% of full-time workers who asked for a raise in the past year got one. But the words you use can quietly cap what you walk away with, long before anyone signs an offer. Knowing what not to say when negotiating your salary matters as much as knowing your ask.

A single throwaway line can anchor you low, tip the balance toward the employer, or make a strong candidate sound unsure. Here are six things to avoid saying, and what to say instead.

Sharing your salary history hands the employer a number to anchor against, and it is almost always lower than what you could negotiate going forward. Pay-transparency laws now bar the question in many states, so you rarely have to answer it.

Recruiters often ask early to set a baseline. Redirect to the market range you want for this role, not what you earned in the last one. Say this instead: "I'm focused on the market rate for this role." As one Implementation Manager on Glassdoor Community noted, "I'd recommend not sharing your current salary. I've found that it can lower offers."

Whoever names a figure first sets the anchor, and that anchor shapes the whole conversation. If you blurt a number before the employer shares a budget, you risk landing under what they were prepared to pay.

Let the employer name the range first. Say this instead: "What range have you budgeted for this role?" Then confirm you're in the ballpark before you talk specifics.

Avoid vague answers, but don't name a random number either. Resolve the tension with timing: when pushed early, offer a researched market range rather than a single figure.

Once you understand the role and hear their range, name a specific, data-backed number in your counter. Say this instead: a market-based range early, a precise figure when you counter. Precision signals you did the homework.

Research your market rate before the conversation; walking in without data usually means underpricing yourself. Many roles now post a range, and workers expect that openness. In a Glassdoor pay transparency poll, 83% of United States (U.S.) employees and job seekers called pay transparency very or somewhat important.¹

Glassdoor chief economist Daniel Zhao writes that pay transparency "helps level the playing field between employers and job seekers." Say this instead: negotiate from market data, not guesswork. Check Glassdoor Salaries to see what your role pays, then build your range from real figures.

Don't accept the moment an offer lands; saying yes ends the negotiation before it starts. Ask for time to review the full offer, then counter, and be ready to walk if it misses your floor.

One more pitfall: get the final number in writing before you sign, so verbal promises don't evaporate. Say this instead: "Thank you, may I take a day to review and get back to you?" An electronic health record (EHR) Trainer on Glassdoor Community said it best: "The secret is to be able to say no."

Apologies and hedges do quiet damage. They signal you don't believe your own ask, and the person across the table hears it. Cut the words that shrink your request:

State your number plainly and let it sit. Say this instead: "Based on my research and experience, I'm targeting $X."

One Scientist I on Glassdoor Community shared what worked: "I didn't apologize, didn't over-explain, just stated it confidently." For a longer list of phrases to cut, see our roundup of 9 things to never say in a salary negotiation.

Put this into practice with people who are negotiating right now. Join Glassdoor Community to compare notes and pressure-test your plan.

Negotiate respectfully and back your ask with research; employers expect it, so a professional counter almost never costs you the offer.

Wait for a written offer, when your negotiating power is highest. Before then, steer the conversation toward their budgeted range.

¹ "Pay Transparency Laws Shine a Light on Salaries," Glassdoor Economic Research / The Harris Poll, Daniel Zhao, November 16, 2022.

#82. More Oversight: California Governor Proposes Independent Watchdogs Within AI Safety System

California Governor Gavin Newsom is proposing a new model of artificial intelligence regulation that would give independent organizations a formal role in evaluating the safety claims made by AI giants.

The effort could eventually include placing outside evaluators inside frontier AI laboratories and requiring companies to maintain an independently tested emergency shutdown mechanism, commonly described as a "kill switch."

Those requirements are not yet California law.

Newsom's Sept. 18 executive order directs state officials to study the proposals and recommend possible changes to existing law by Nov. 16. It does not immediately require OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or other developers to install a shutdown mechanism.

The distinction matters because the phrase "AI kill switch" suggests a technical safeguard California has already imposed. For now, it is one element of a broader oversight system the state is assembling around the developers of its most powerful AI models.

Under the order, the California Government Operations Agency and the Governor's Office of Emergency Services must consult outside experts about whether the state should require large frontier developers to embed independent verification organizations in their laboratories.

The evaluators could conduct periodic audits and determine whether company safety frameworks and risk assessments meet adequate standards. They could also test whether an emergency shutdown mechanism would work as intended.

The order asks officials to consider expanding the definition of a reportable critical safety incident to include cases in which an AI system appears to evade controls or operate beyond its intended boundaries.

Newsom said the action was prompted by recent incidents involving AI agents defeating security restrictions, as well as the absence of comprehensive federal legislation.

"We're not waiting to act," Newsom said in the state's announcement of the order. "We're going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it's too late."

The executive order builds on two laws Newsom signed on Sept. 9. Together, Senate Bill 813 and Assembly Bill 1405 begin regulating the organizations hired to inspect AI systems.

California's earlier frontier AI law, SB 53, requires large developers to publish safety frameworks and report specified critical incidents. The new laws begin addressing a separate question: Who checks whether those disclosures and assessments are reliable?

SB 813 requires the Government Operations Agency to develop standards for designating independent verification organizations, or IVOs. Those organizations must demonstrate that they have the expertise to assess AI risks and explain the measurements and methods supporting their conclusions.

#84. 2 ways a Michigan district builds unity during the budgeting process

Let K-12 Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Activities that break silos, build understanding and explore hypotheticals are key, two district leaders told attendees at ASBO’s annual conference.

PITTSBURGH — In Michigan’s Livingston Educational Service Agency, the budgeting process doesn’t fall solely on the school system’s finance office, administrators say.

Instead, Livingston ESA prioritizes developing relationships across departments within its leadership cabinet to build trust as they craft their own budget spending, said Stephanie Weese, the district’s deputy superintendent.

This relationship-building allows the 28,000-student district to better understand departmental needs and also be more transparent within its leadership team, she said.

The process has helped the district forecast and create a very accurate budget for the upcoming school year, Weese said. That success is because the district is “talking to people and figuring out what’s needed and what works and what doesn’t work,” she said, and it’s “not just making the numbers more accurate by looking at trends.”

During a Wednesday presentation at the Association of School Business Officials International’s 2026 Annual Conference & Expo in Pittsburgh, Weese and Livingston ESA Superintendent Michael Hubert shared how the district taps into relationship-building to ultimately improve its budgeting process.

Livingston ESA’s leadership team typically meets twice per month, and the budget director also attends to provide timely updates on the district’s finances, Weese said.

During those meetings, each person shares — at most — three key, short updates from their departments, Hubert said. This approach is something he describes as “connect the dots.”

Simple updates like this are important, Hubert said, because they provide every leader with more context about what’s happening across the district. If the district were to enter a stressful financial period that would require budget cuts, he said, that additional information becomes even more useful for department leaders to engage with each other on any difficult decision-making down the line.

Before district leaders “connect the dots” during the meeting, they also share their appreciation and check in with each other, Hubert said. Ahead of the meeting, each member of the leadership team also fills out a pre-check-in short form that Hubert reviews so he can understand what issues need more discussion.

“How we build the trust is by respecting each other and engaging and listening to who they are, how they're engaging in their work, [and] what's going on,” Hubert said.

Even though Livingston ESA has not had to make budget cuts as of late, Hubert said, it’s important that his leadership team knows how to make reductions if necessary.

To build on those skills, the cabinet collectively engages in a cost-cutting exercise where each member closely examines their individual budgets. While the exercise allowed leaders to look at their budgets in detail, Weese said one con was that the practice “really didn’t feel real.”

That’s because some leaders whose departments are fully funded through grants would push back that they don’t need to make cuts and would point to another department that could make cuts more easily, she said.

When the budget director provides updates to the leadership team with the district’s financial outlook for the next year, the director will also identify the status of that budget projection as a red, yellow or green light, Weese said. Green signifies steady or increased funding, yellow means the district should be cautious about adding new expenses, and red signals that the district should consider making budget cuts.

That model extends to mid-year budget reviews. If the district has extra funds available in its budget after adjustments are made, the cabinet would propose and review additional line items for their respective departments. Hubert would then approve, discuss or reject a proposal with similar green, yellow or red light language.

Weese said that exercise helped improve engagement across the leadership team, though it was a time-consuming effort that requires advance planning.

“They all had the opportunity to add their wants, their needs, and we then talked about it as an entire cabinet,” Weese said.
