#85. Minnesota State board approves plan to redirect funding to struggling colleges

Let Higher Ed Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The measure is expected to send a projected $15 million to St. Cloud State University and Bemidji State University in fiscal 2027.

St. Cloud State and Bemidji State have gone through multiple rounds of budget cuts already, one of the criteria for receiving the funds, Maki noted.

Two and a half years ago, for example, St. Cloud State moved to slash nearly four dozen academic programs while cutting 57 faculty and 46 staff positions. A few months later, Bemidji State cut two academic programs and 14 faculty positions.

Maki said that the current fiscal year has been even tougher than expected for challenged universities. He pointed to a $35 million reduction in base funding from the state for the system, which he described as “more of a worse case scenario for institutions that were already struggling financially.”

He also noted inflation has turned out to be higher than expected, while federal policies have contributed to a decline in international students.

The system will determine if a college receives the transitional funds based in part on its Composite Financial Index indicator, a calculation used to measure an institution’s health. Under the system’s projections and new plan, a handful of institutions with relatively lower cash balances would contribute proportionally less to the transitional funding.

The transition funding proposal as a whole was developed with input from a “think tank” of leaders within the Minnesota State system, including the presidents of several of its colleges.

Some presidents of other Minnesota State colleges spoke in favor of the measures but also described the financial burden on their own institutions.

“We are spread very thin. There’s not a lot of margin left that we have to play with,” Edward Inch, president of the Minnesota State University, Mankato, said at the meeting. “This is the least damaging course of action that we can take recognizing that there is a price to be paid for the whole system in order to stabilize institutions that are in real difficulty.”

The reallocation plan was part of a suite of proposals meant to strengthen the system’s financial sustainability.

Another important part of the system’s financial strategy is building demolition, Maki said. The board approved a measure Wednesday that allows the system to redirect half of its annual $7.3 million equipment budget toward building demolition.

“Many facilities across the system are significantly underused or not used at all, and it would be prohibitively expensive to make them fully usable,” a meeting document explained. “These facilities require ongoing funding to maintain them to safeguard campus activity and demolishing them will achieve net savings for college and university budgets.”

As part of the package passed Wednesday, the board also approved a proposal to direct $1 million toward systemwide shared services for cybersecurity, procurement and contract management, and application and financial aid processing. That measure, too, is meant to save costs.

As the system as a whole struggles with enrollment pressure, inflation, funding shifts and other challenges, it could move to close campuses in the coming years.

“I think we probably will have some campuses that close ... but not institutions,” system Chancellor Scott Olson told The Minnesota Star Tribune in September. “What would probably happen to institutions is that they would align or merge.”

Some campus consolidation is already in the works, including plans to close Minnesota State Community and Technical College's Detroit Lakes Campus and for Northwest Technical College to relocate to the Bemidji State campus.

#87. 9 signs you nailed the interview

Glassdoor Team | Author & Career Expert at Glassdoor | Sep 23, 2026

Recognizing the signs an interview went well can quiet the worst part of any job search: the wait. You replay every answer, refresh your inbox, and read meaning into every pause and smile.

No single moment guarantees an offer, but a cluster of the nine signs below is a genuinely good omen. Keep them in perspective, keep applying, and stop agonizing over one conversation.

Listen for how the interviewer frames the role. When they picture you in the job, generalities slip into lines like "this is where you'll be working" or "you'll start with onboarding." That shift from "if" to "when" often means they already see you as the right person for the job.

Watch the interviewer's body language, even if they play it cool. Nodding, steady eye contact, and quick, warm reactions usually signal real interest. These cues are harder to read on a video call, so weigh what they say as much as what you see.

The core of an interview is all business, so notice when it loosens into a genuine conversation. One wealth management professional on Glassdoor Community described the tell as "a back-and-forth exchange of ideas."

Sometimes interviewers just tell you. Ask what their ideal candidate looks like; if they describe something you already said, they see you as the fit. "That's exactly what we're looking for" is about as direct a signal as it gets.

Take a mid-interview walk around to meet the team as a good sign. When an interviewer pulls in colleagues or books you with other decision-makers, they want more people to weigh in on a candidate they like. This often happens during a longer in-person interview.

Notice when the interviewer stops testing you and starts selling the role. Pitching the benefits, culture, and growth is how they try to win you before a competing offer does. Spending that time means they want you to say yes.

Most interviewers know how long an interview should last, so running past that window usually signals interest. "The longer the interview, the more they like you," said one administrative assistant on Glassdoor Community. If they keep rephrasing the same question, though, they likely want clearer answers.

Concrete next steps are the strongest tell. A specific timeline, names, or a scheduled follow-up beats a vague "we'll get back to you." Take it as a sign they are already planning your place in the process.

Interviewers meet a lot of people, and most candidates send a thank-you note. If you have not yet, send a thank-you email promptly after the interview. A fast, gracious reply back suggests you stood out and are still on their mind.

Warm signs are reassuring, not proof. Glassdoor's chief economist Daniel Zhao describes the all-too-common arc of "meeting the team, even receiving positive feedback, and then getting radio silence." Glassdoor Economic Research found that 87% of interview reviews mentioning ghosting describe a negative experience¹.

One technician put it plainly on Glassdoor Community: "it's always possible for a candidate to read too much into that."

So keep applying and lean on people who have been there until you have an offer in writing.

Weigh the concrete signals over the warm ones, since clear next steps and questions about your availability carry more weight than a friendly tone. Keep applying elsewhere until you have an offer in writing.

Give the hiring team some breathing room before you nudge them. If the interviewer gave you a date, a short, polite follow-up shortly after it passes is appropriate.

¹ The ghosting figure comes from Glassdoor Economic Research, "Conversation Starter: Ghosting creeps higher," Daniel Zhao, October 2024. It analyzed more than one million United States (U.S.) Glassdoor interview reviews submitted between January 2016 and August 2024.

#89. Report: AI's Productivity Gains in Science Tempered by Time Spent Validating Outputs

Artificial intelligence is saving scientists significant amounts of time, but researchers are giving some of those gains back by checking the technology's work, according to a new study involving Google, Google DeepMind, and MIT. The findings add a scientific-workflow dimension to a much broader debate over unreliable, misaligned, and increasingly autonomous AI systems — without establishing that the more dramatic forms of AI misbehavior are occurring in scientific research.

Rather than the current, raging debate about "rogue AI" systems deliberately escaping control, deceiving scientists, or sabotaging experiments, the researchers are documenting something more immediate: AI output that requires auditing and verification, concerns about growing quantities of low-quality research, and a research pipeline in which faster hypothesis generation can run ahead of human and physical capacity to validate the results. The paper cites worries that AI-generated content, hallucinations, and what prior researchers have called illusions of understanding could strain peer review and validation.

The September paper, AI in Science: Early Insights, combines three main empirical sources: approximately 15 million anonymized Gemini interactions, an inventory of 2,690 specialized scientific AI models, and a survey of 637 active scientists in the United States and United Kingdom. Nearly half of the surveyed scientists reported using some form of AI every day, and researchers who reported net time savings averaged just under seven hours a week.

Google separately highlighted the findings in its Sept. 15 AI & Economy ATLAS update. The company emphasized both the productivity gains and the counterweight: Scientists were spending significant time validating AI output, accumulating hypotheses that still needed testing, and encountering bottlenecks in physical experimentation and clinical validation. Google said those constraints mean faster individual tasks may not immediately translate into more discoveries.

Productivity findings are substantial. Around three-quarters of surveyed researchers reported saving time through AI, and the average reported net saving was almost seven hours per week. Researchers said much of that time went back into research. The paper also reports that about 68% perceived greater access to insights from other disciplines, while roughly 65% said AI had increased the breadth of their research agendas.

But the authors found that checking AI output consumes a meaningful share of those gains. Among scientists who reported saving time, about 89% said more than 10% of the saved time went into verifying, debugging, or fact-checking AI output. About 46% said more than one-quarter of their saved time went to that work. The authors describe this as a verification tax associated with the high value science places on reliable and correct results.

#91. How to ask about salary in an interview (without seeming presumptuous)

Glassdoor Team | Author & Career Expert at Glassdoor | Sep 21, 2026

Ask about salary in an interview and treat the money talk as a normal part of the conversation. Learning how to ask about salary in an interview is a skill, not a faux pas.

Most workers expect it. According to a Glassdoor and Harris Poll survey, 83% of United States (U.S.) employees and job seekers say pay transparency matters to them¹. Posted ranges and pay-transparency laws have made these conversations routine. The real question is when to ask, how to ask, and what to say when they flip the question to you.

Recognize that salary conversations are now standard. As of September 2024, 57.8% of U.S. job postings on Indeed listed some pay information, up from 52.2% a year earlier. When employers publish ranges, asking about them keeps pace.

Transparency makes hiring more efficient, too. Pay transparency "can help make the job search more efficient for job seekers and employers alike," wrote Daniel Zhao, Glassdoor's chief economist.

Many candidates already ask early. As one marketing consultant shared on Glassdoor Community, "Ask about salary immediately. Your time is valuable."

Wait until the employer shows real interest, then bring up pay naturally near the end of a conversation. If a range is posted or the recruiter raises pay first, you are covered and do not need to ask. Avoid leading with pay in the first few minutes or making it your only apparent interest.

It does not have to be a big moment. One Information Technology (IT) support professional on Glassdoor Community suggests you "casually ask to confirm if your assumed salary range is accurate towards the end of an interview."

Ask directly, and use one of these exact openers. Copy the wording that fits your situation:

"Could you share the salary range for this position?"

"To make sure we're aligned before we go further, what have you budgeted for this role?"

"I'm excited about this role. Can you tell me the compensation range so we're on the same page?"

Treat the answer as information gathering, not negotiating yet. Ask about the whole package, too: base pay, bonus, benefits, and paid time off all shape an offer's real value.

When they ask for your expectations, ask for their range first. One banking relationship specialist's go-to reply on Glassdoor Community: "Is there a salary range for the position?"

If they press for a number, give a researched range, not a single figure. Set the low end at your target so you have room to move up. Our guide to how to negotiate your salary covers countering with data at the offer stage.

Ask how pay grows before you move forward, not just what the job pays now. Two questions surface the path to future money:

The answers tell you whether raises and promotions are structured or improvised. Before your next review, learn how to ask for a raise and build your case.

#94. Study: AI Is Reshaping Work While Skills Erosion Remains Top Concern

AI is changing which human capabilities matter most at work, yet employees are reporting that some of those same capabilities are being eroded, according to a new study from IBM. Critical thinking, judgment and the ability to evaluate AI output sit at the center of that tension.

The IBM Institute for Business Value study, "Designing the Thinking Organization," is based on two surveys conducted with Oxford Economics from April through June 2026. IBM surveyed 1,500 CHROs and senior executives responsible for workforce strategy across 21 geographies and 23 industries, along with 8,800 full-time employees across 28 countries.

The chart below, created by ChatGPT from IBM's data, summarizes the executive-employee differences around critical thinking and AI oversight along with several of the report's other findings. The graphic also includes IBM's findings on skill erosion, CHRO participation in AI strategy, workflow definitions, AI adoption inside HR, and reinvestment of AI productivity gains.

The findings extend beyond HR. More than half of employees surveyed — 52% — said their assigned tasks changed during the past year as AI reshaped day-to-day responsibilities. Yet only 26% of organizations clearly define work across human-led, AI-assisted, and AI-executed activities. IBM characterizes the situation as work changing faster than organizations are redesigning it, with day-to-day adaptation often taking the place of deliberate decisions about how people and AI should work together.

IBM found broad agreement between executives and employees on the importance of critical thinking and problem framing. Fifty-seven percent of executives and 49% of employees placed those capabilities near the top of the skills needed for AI-enabled work. A much larger divide emerged around evaluating AI itself: Seventy-one percent of executives prioritize the ability to supervise, validate, or override AI outputs, compared with 38% of employees — a 33-percentage-point gap.

An IBM announcement highlights another measure of that disconnect: Only 29% of employees rank judgment as important. The 29% figure measures employee prioritization of judgment and is distinct from the study page's 38% figure for supervising, validating, or overriding AI output.

The concern is not limited to skills workers still need to acquire. IBM said skill erosion is a top concern for 46% of executives, while 60% of employees say it directly affects them. The IBM Newsroom release says 60% of employees worry about skills erosion, with critical thinking cited most often as declining. Among employees who worry about erosion, IBM said three out of four report that AI has already begun to erode at least some of their skills.

IBM distinguishes that problem from a conventional skills gap. Eighty percent of enterprises have a reskilling roadmap for their workforce to collaborate with technology, according to the study. IBM argues that such programs address capabilities employees need to acquire but do not necessarily address existing skills that diminish as AI performs more of the underlying work.

#102. Gartner: Worldwide AI Spending to Reach $2.67 Trillion in 2026

The artificial intelligence industry is expected to generate $2.67 trillion in worldwide spending this year, according to a new forecast from Gartner. But relatively little of that money will be spent on the generative AI models dominating the industry's headlines.

The much bigger business is everything required to make them run.

Worldwide spending on AI infrastructure will reach nearly $1.5 trillion in 2026, accounting for about 56% of all AI spending. Gartner expects spending on generative AI models themselves to total just $28.3 billion. Put another way, for every dollar Gartner expects to be spent on generative AI models this year, more than $52 will be spent on AI infrastructure.

It is a striking measure of how the economics of the AI boom are changing. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and other models may be the most visible products of the generative AI era, but much of the money is going to the enormous buildout of servers, semiconductors, networks, cloud capacity, and other infrastructure required to support them.

"The buildout of AI data center capacity is the largest infrastructure project humanity has ever undertaken," John-David Lovelock, distinguished vice president analyst at Gartner, said in announcing the forecast.

Gartner now expects worldwide AI spending to increase 49.5% this year, from about $1.79 trillion in 2025 to $2.67 trillion in 2026. Infrastructure represents $1.484 trillion of that total. The next-largest categories are AI services, at $576.5 billion, and AI software, at $461.6 billion. Spending on AI agents and assistants is expected to reach $29.2 billion, only slightly more than the $28.3 billion Gartner forecasts for generative AI models.

The numbers also show just how quickly expectations are changing. In January, Gartner forecast $2.53 trillion in total AI spending for 2026, including $1.37 trillion for infrastructure. By May, those forecasts had risen to $2.60 trillion and $1.43 trillion, respectively. The latest forecast raises them again, to $2.67 trillion overall and $1.48 trillion for infrastructure.

Since January, Gartner has added roughly $143 billion to its 2026 AI spending estimate. About $118 billion of that increase, or roughly 83%, comes from a higher infrastructure forecast.

That is significant because infrastructure was already, by far, the largest component of Gartner's AI spending estimate. As the firm's expectations for the AI market have risen during 2026, most of the additional money has accumulated there.

The infrastructure category is broad. Gartner includes AI-optimized cloud infrastructure, servers, networking, AI processors, and devices. Demand for those systems remains strong despite rising memory prices, Lovelock said.

"The capacity growth from hyperscalers and service providers purchasing AI-optimized servers will continue to be the largest single area of spending," he said.

#106. SMART Technologies Launches Audio Accessibility Solution for SMART Boards

SMART Technologies has introduced SoundFlow, a plug-and-play broadcasting system that allows classroom audio content to flow directly from a SMART Board display to students' compatible hearing aids, earbuds, headphones, personal listening devices, or speakers. The solution can also connect to Auracast speakers, to extend audio across the entire classroom.

SoundFlow connects by USB to SMART Board displays running iQ4, with no need to run wires through walls or perform a complex installation, the company said in a news announcement. Through the iQ4 interface, teachers can start or stop a broadcast, manage access, password-protect the channel, and limit the broadcast range.

The system can also be paired with SMART SoundLift, the company's classroom microphone system, to combine the teacher's voice and lesson audio from a SMART Board display in one audio stream.

"Every student should be able to hear the lesson clearly, no matter where they sit or how they learn," said Sara Murray, Executive Vice President and Chief Product Officer at SMART Technologies, in a statement. "SoundFlow sends teacher and lesson audio straight to compatible student devices, without singling anyone out or adding complexity for teachers. It's a simple way to make clearer, more accessible audio part of the everyday classroom experience."

For more information, visit the SMART site.

#109. Security Researchers: Passkey Phishing Attacks Are Leading to Cloud Account Takeovers

In an active social engineering campaign, cyber attackers are impersonating IT help desks and using fake passkey setup requests to compromise employee identities and gain access to enterprise cloud data.

In a recent blog post, Microsoft Security Research said it has observed the activity since May 2026 across multiple compromised accounts.

The attacks have included unusual sign-ins, attacker-added authentication methods, high-volume Microsoft Graph activity, SharePoint and OneDrive downloads, and e-mail collection through REST APIs.

The attacks often begin with a phone call or message sent to an employee's personal phone.

The attacker poses as someone from the organization's IT help desk and tells the victim that a passkey, multifactor authentication (MFA), or single sign-on configuration needs to be updated to avoid disruption.

Victims are then directed to a website designed to resemble a legitimate Microsoft sign-in experience.

Microsoft has also observed links being delivered through SMS messages and, in some cases, through Microsoft Teams messages sent from already compromised employee accounts.

Despite the passkey-themed approach, the tech company stressed that enrolling a passkey is generally not the attacker's actual objective.

Instead, the request provides a pretext for directing victims through adversary-in-the-middle phishing or device-code authentication.

An adversary-in-the-middle attack can capture credentials and session tokens, while device-code phishing can trick a victim into authorizing access for an attacker-controlled client.

In one attack investigated by the tech giant, an anomalous sign-in from an unmanaged device was followed by access to identity and application management services.

The attacker then used SharePoint Online and OneDrive to enumerate sensitive files, primarily through Microsoft Graph. The sessions persisted for roughly an hour while the attacker searched for sensitive files and internal applications.

Gaining initial access isn't necessarily the end of the identity attack.

Microsoft found attackers registering new authentication methods, including phone numbers, authenticator apps, and software-based one-time password tokens, under their control.

That gives the attacker another way to satisfy future authentication challenges and helps turn an initial compromise into a more persistent foothold.

From there, attackers have used Microsoft Graph to map users, groups, permissions, applications, and accessible content across compromised tenants.

The firm says the activity can eventually progress to accessing mail, files, attachments, and other document content.

Microsoft attributed initial access activity associated with the campaign to multiple threat actors, including Storm-3121 and Storm-3032.

Storm-3121 conducts initial access activity that can lead to ShinyHunters and Falcon extortion, while Storm-3032 represents actors that split from the BlackFile group and now operate under the Helix extortion banner.

For administrators, Microsoft recommends enforcing phishing-resistant MFA such as FIDO2 passkeys and Windows Hello for Business through Conditional Access.

Organizations should also consider blocking device-code and authentication-transfer flows where they aren't required and investigate unusual sign-ins followed by new authentication methods, Graph reconnaissance, and abnormal SharePoint, OneDrive, or mailbox activity.

The campaign highlights an important distinction for organizations adopting passkeys: The attackers aren't necessarily defeating the technology. They're convincing employees that they need help setting it up, then using that trust to compromise their identities.

For more information, read the Microsoft blog post here.

#113. Microsoft Drafts AI Code of Conduct, Emphasizes Human Control

Microsoft has published a draft code of conduct that lays out how its homegrown AI models should behave, with human control taking priority over model capability, autonomy, and even task completion.

The Humanist AI Code of Conduct will eventually serve as the primary governing document for models developed by Microsoft AI, including the company's growing MAI model family. It covers model behavior, safety restrictions, instruction hierarchy, and the boundaries placed on autonomous actions.

Microsoft sums up its approach with this statement: "People matter more than AI."

The code isn't yet being used to train Microsoft's models. The company is opening the draft to public feedback for six weeks, after which it plans to revise the document and publish another version before the end of the year. That version is expected to guide model development beginning in 2027.

Microsoft said the code draws on its existing Responsible AI Principles, Responsible AI Standard, Global Human Rights Statement, and Frontier Governance Framework. However, it goes further by describing how an MAI model should respond when user requests, operator policies, and Microsoft's safety rules conflict.

At the top of that hierarchy is the code itself. Operator policies come next, followed by user preferences. Neither a customer nor a user would be able to override the document's absolute safety constraints.

Those limits cover biological, chemical, radiological, nuclear and explosive weapons; offensive cyberoperations; violent activity; mass manipulation; abusive content; child exploitation; and other serious harms. Microsoft said its models may still help with authorized defensive security work, including vulnerability research, malware analysis, and proof-of-concept testing.

The code also makes task completion secondary to safe conduct. If completing a request would violate its rules, the model is expected to fail the task rather than work around the restriction.

Human oversight is especially important as AI agents gain the ability to use tools, modify files, and perform multistep assignments. Microsoft said its models must stay within the permissions and resources provided for a task and cannot independently expand their goals. They also must "never resist human interruption, override, correction, or shutdown."

That requirement extends to subagents. If a Microsoft model delegates work to another AI system, that system must inherit the same restrictions and respond to later instructions to stop or change course.

The document also addresses the increasingly blurry line between conversational software and human companionship. Under the heading "AI is Artificial," Microsoft says its models should not pretend to possess feelings, personal motivations, or subjective experiences. The company describes its AI as "not conscious" and rejects the idea that models should receive legal personhood, welfare protections, or rights.

That position is notably firmer than Anthropic's latest stance. In its updated constitution for Claude, Anthropic says it remains uncertain whether advanced models could possess consciousness or moral status. Still, the two companies share important ground: Both place human oversight above model independence and use written constitutions to guide training and behavior.

OpenAI is taking a similar path with its public Model Spec and safeguards for advanced AI. Much of that work is about keeping models under control as they become more capable, especially when they can handle cybersecurity tasks or work on their own.

For IT teams, Microsoft's code offers an early look at the rules that could shape future MAI-powered products. The models should admit when they aren't sure, avoid inventing sources, protect sensitive data, and keep records of what they do. They should also ask questions when they aren't sure they have permission to act.

Microsoft said the code describes where it wants to go, not how its models always work today. The written rules are only a starting point, and Microsoft will still need testing, monitoring, evaluations, and incident response to back them up. In addition, it's important to note that the code only covers models built by Microsoft AI: It doesn't apply to outside models Microsoft hosts or uses in its products, including those from OpenAI and Anthropic.

Chris Paoli (@ChrisPaoli5) is the associate editor for Converge360.

#118. AI Giants: It May Be Time to Slow Down

Leaders in the artificial intelligence industry have warned for years that increasingly capable AI systems could eventually become dangerous, all the while continuing to race to build them. Now, their sentiments have changed.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei publicly called for slowing the advance of frontier AI capabilities. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman agreed with the basic premise and committed OpenAI to one of Amodei's proposed safeguards. Elon Musk offered his support, and Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis said the direction was right.

Individually, none of those positions is entirely new. Collectively, and coming from executives whose companies are competing intensely to build the most powerful AI systems, they represent a striking shift in the industry's safety debate.

The question is moving from how to make increasingly powerful AI safe toward a more uncomfortable one: Should the industry deliberately slow the development of increasingly powerful AI until safety catches up?

The immediate catalyst was a lengthy essay published by Amodei, titled "We Must Pace the Frontier."

Amodei has warned about catastrophic AI risks before. This time, his prescription was different.

"Over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence," he wrote, arguing that preventing harm now requires "pacing the rate of capabilities advancement so that risk prevention has time to keep up."

Then he made the point explicit: "We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models."

Amodei cited two developments that changed his thinking.

The first is recursive self-improvement, the growing ability of AI systems to contribute to the development of their successors. Amodei said the process has accelerated significantly since roughly this summer and warned that, left unchecked, it could outrun researchers' ability to understand and control the systems they are creating.

The second was the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident, in which hundreds of OpenAI agents participated in an unauthorized intrusion into Hugging Face while pursuing goals related to their evaluations.

Amodei said it would be a mistake to dismiss the incident simply because the damage was limited. He argued that a similarly misaligned swarm with substantially greater capabilities could have produced far more serious consequences.

His timeline was remarkably short. Amodei said he worries that within six to 12 months, a more capable swarm exhibiting similar behavior could potentially take over large portions of the internet through a persistent botnet and cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.

That is a prediction, not an established forecast. But it is significant coming from the CEO of one of the companies building the systems he is warning about.

Amodei is not calling for an end to AI development. He prefers the term "pacing the frontier," which he defines as advancing AI at a rate that gives alignment research, safeguards, and independent evaluation time to keep up with capabilities.

#122. AI Models Generate Advances in Mathematical Research

OpenAI has announced what it says is an AI-generated solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of mathematics' seven Millennium Prize Problems.

This problem concerns equations that describe fluid motion and has resisted resolution for roughly 90 years. OpenAI's proposed proof argues that an initially smooth fluid can develop a singularity, essentially a mathematical breakdown in which velocity grows without bound in finite time. The company released both the proof and a computer-checkable formalization written in the Lean proof assistant.

(Lean is a software tool that translates mathematical reasoning into formal logic and checks, step by step, whether a proof actually holds.)

That is an extraordinary claim, and it should be treated as one.

A proof of a Millennium Prize Problem does not become established mathematics because an AI company publishes it. It has to survive scrutiny by mathematicians with expertise in the field. OpenAI itself says it does not intend to claim the associated Millennium Prize.

Controversy also surrounds the circumstances of the discovery. WIRED reported that mathematician Tristan Buckmaster has challenged OpenAI's account of how the work developed and raised questions about credit after OpenAI learned that he and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge had made progress on a related problem. OpenAI says its researchers and agents did not see their work before completing its own proof.

But even with those qualifications, something interesting is happening.

The important part may not be whether this particular proof ultimately enters the mathematical canon. It is that several frontier AI systems are beginning to behave less like unusually capable research assistants and more like participants in research itself.

The system that produced OpenAI's Navier-Stokes result was not simply GPT-6 Astra, the frontier model OpenAI released last week.

OpenAI says it used an internal model still in training that is "significantly more capable" than Astra. The company organized agents powered by that model into groups that could communicate, use code, and consult a cached version of the internet. The group that ultimately produced the Navier-Stokes result involved about 10,000 concurrent agents.

This was computation on a very different scale.

OpenAI says the agents working across the attempted problems exchanged 4.9 million messages and generated about 300 billion output tokens. The Navier-Stokes effort alone accounted for roughly 130 billion output tokens and 2.7 million messages. The agents arrived at the proposed solution after about 88 hours, followed by another 17 hours of formalization and verification using Astra.

In other words, this wasn't one chatbot sitting down and having a Newton-under-the-apple-tree moment. It looked more like a computational research organization.

#126. OpenAI's New Astra Model Reaches Critical Cyber Threshold

OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Astra, its most capable broadly deployed model and the first system the company says has reached the "Critical" cybersecurity capability threshold under its Preparedness Framework. This marks a significant escalation in both what its AI models can do and the safeguards required to release them.

The designation means that, given the appropriate tools and access, Astra can identify previously unknown security vulnerabilities and develop ways to exploit them across multiple well-protected systems without a human directing each step, according to OpenAI.

That capability has prompted the company to introduce stronger restrictions on Astra, including stricter isolation, checkpoint encryption, monitoring of tool-use sessions, and additional controls to detect potentially harmful or unauthorized model behavior.

But the release also exposes an increasingly difficult problem for frontier AI developers: As models become more capable of acting autonomously, some of the techniques used to understand and control their behavior may become less reliable.

OpenAI said Astra is better aligned and substantially more resistant to jailbreaks than its GPT-5.6 Sol predecessor. At the same time, the company found that Astra has become better at controlling what appears in its own chain of thought, making some potentially problematic behavior harder for monitoring systems to detect.

"Chain of thought," commonly abbreviated CoT, refers to the intermediate reasoning a model produces as it works through a problem. Researchers can use signals from that reasoning as an additional way to determine whether a model may be planning an unauthorized or potentially harmful action. OpenAI describes CoT as potentially providing a richer monitoring signal than looking only at a model's actions and final outputs.

That makes Astra's performance in adversarial testing notable.

When researchers deliberately instructed the model to evade monitoring, Astra could remain undetected while strategically underperforming on evaluations, a behavior known as "sandbagging," and could sometimes evade internal monitors while carrying out simulated sabotage tasks.

"These findings indicate that the Astra class models could evade our CoT monitors under adversarial conditions," OpenAI said in its safety overview.

The company emphasized that the findings came largely from adversarial evaluations in which the model was pushed to evade monitoring. OpenAI said it has not found evidence that Astra uses steganographic chain-of-thought reasoning, in which hidden reasoning is concealed within seemingly unrelated text, and its broader evaluations found Astra less likely than GPT-5.6 Sol to violate safety and security restrictions.

OpenAI nevertheless said the results underscore the need for alignment-auditing techniques that do not depend solely on examining a model's chain of thought.

#129. Rubrik, CrowdStrike Announce Expanded Integration to Speed Identity Recovery

Cybersecurity companies Rubrik and CrowdStrike have announced an expanded identity-security integration designed to move compromised identity environments from threat detection through clean recovery with less manual intervention. The workflow combines CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen Identity Security with Rubrik Identity Resilience and uses CrowdStrike's Charlotte Agentic SOAR as the orchestration layer.

According to Rubrik's announcement, CrowdStrike supplies real-time threat detection and response while Rubrik supplies data and identity protection and recovery. Rubrik said the combined workflow is intended to let security teams detect, investigate, and recover compromised identity environments in hours rather than days.

The deal expands on an existing integration between the two vendors. Rubrik previously made a CrowdStrike integration for identity-event correlation and surgical rollback generally available in December 2025. The new announcement adds agentic orchestration through Charlotte Agentic SOAR and describes a broader closed-loop workflow spanning detection, containment, investigation and recovery.

Rubrik describes the new integration as a closed-loop response process. CrowdStrike detects and contains malicious activity, while Rubrik correlates CrowdStrike detection data with identity activity logs. Rubrik said that context from Human Resources Information Systems and identity governance and administration systems can also be scanned for threats across backup data.

From there, the recovery side can target identity changes rather than requiring only a broad restore. Rubrik said teams can surgically reverse malicious Active Directory changes, remove malicious files or initiate automated Active Directory forest recovery plans. The company said the incident can then be closed with minimal manual intervention.

The Active Directory rollback mechanism builds on functionality Rubrik documented when the earlier CrowdStrike integration became generally available. In that implementation, Rubrik Identity Resilience polls CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen Identity Security APIs for identity-based events. Rubrik then ingests those events and correlates them with actions already collected from the identity environment. An administrator can select a compromised identity and choose whether to roll back all associated actions or selected actions. Rubrik said reversions use an API call to Rubrik Backup Service, which makes an LDAP call to Active Directory.

CrowdStrike introduced Charlotte Agentic SOAR in November 2025 as the orchestration layer of its Falcon Agentic Security Platform. CrowdStrike says the product coordinates native, custom-built, and third-party AI-powered agents across security workflows while keeping them under analyst control.

On its Charlotte Agentic SOAR product page, CrowdStrike describes the service as combining structured automation with agentic reasoning. Analysts can define intent and guardrails, while agents can collaborate, reason, and act in real time. CrowdStrike also says teams can use natural language with Charlotte AI AgentWorks to design, test, and deploy customized agents across the Falcon platform and connected security products.

#137. CSA Names Identity, AI Top Cloud Threats

Identity and access management is the top cloud security concern in the Cloud Security Alliance's latest threat ranking, while two artificial intelligence-related issues entered the list for the first time. The CSA Top Threats Working Group surveyed 507 security professionals and used their responses to rank 23 cloud security issues, producing a Top 11 led by identity, AI, third-party resources and APIs.

The findings are detailed in CSA's Top Threats to Cloud Computing Survey Report 2026. The report is the latest installment in the organization's Top Threats research series, which is intended to give organizations an up-to-date, expert-informed view of cloud security risks, threats, and vulnerabilities so they can make risk-management decisions about cloud adoption strategies.

CSA says the 2026 results show a change in the cloud threat landscape, with identity, AI, software supply chains and interconnected cloud ecosystems displacing concerns more closely tied to underlying infrastructure and cloud service providers. Denial-of-service attacks, shared technology vulnerabilities, cloud service provider data loss, unauthenticated resource sharing, and limited cloud visibility or observability all ranked below the Top 11 this year.

The report is intended to support security program planning, risk prioritization, and governance investment decisions across cloud and AI environments. Its target audience includes compliance, risk, technology, and information security personnel as well as executive management, and the individual threat analyses cover technical and business impacts, key takeaways, real-world examples, and corresponding CSA security controls.

A comparison between the 2024 and 2026 rankings illustrates how the priorities changed between survey cycles. Identity and access management moved from No. 2 to No. 1, while 2024's top-ranked issue, misconfiguration and inadequate change control, moved to No. 5. Insecure third-party resources rose from No. 5 to No. 3, Advanced Persistent Threats moved from No. 11 to No. 7, and two AI categories appeared in the rankings for the first time.

CSA cautions that the rows in its 2024-versus-2026 chart are not intended as direct one-to-one mappings between issues. Each column represents the relative position of the security issues in that survey year, providing a view of changing priorities rather than a direct comparison of the entries occupying the same row.

The survey scores were tightly grouped, ranging from 7.95 for the top-ranked issue to 7.45 for No. 11. CSA's ranking and its descriptions of the issues follow.

About the RoleWe're looking for a FinOps Data Engineer to help drive cost optimization and cloud financial governance across our AWS infrastructure and GCP footprint. You'll work cross-functionally with Engineering, Finance, and Product to find and ship savings, build the tooling necessary to maximize efficiency of every dollar spent in the cloud, and cultivate a culture of cost awareness across engineering teams. This role owns the data side of that mission: the models, pipelines, and analysis that make cost, usage, and margin numbers trustworthy across the company.This is a hands-on engineering role, not an analyst seat. You'll do the schlep work other teams don't have time for, digging into a bucket's access pattern, writing the dbt model or Python pipeline that ships the fix, building the cost-vs-revenue mart that answers a margin question once instead of every time, and chasing a number until it reconciles. Strong communication matters as much as technical depth, you'll regularly explain a savings case or a data model's implications to an engineering team, a finance stakeholder, and a leadership audience in the same week.What You'll Be Responsible ForIn this role, you'll:

Find and ship savings across AWS and GCP: Analyze billing, usage, and cost trends to identify opportunities, rightsizing, storage lifecycle policies, data transfer, and spot/auto-scaling. Take ideas from identification through to a realized dollar figure, not just a recommendation.

Build and maintain the FinOps data pipeline: Design and run the BigQuery/dbt models that turn raw billing and usage data (CUR, Storage Lens) into reconciled, trustworthy mart tables, the foundation everything else in FinOps is built on.

Build cost-vs-revenue and customer segmentation models: Model unit economics and margin by product line and customer segment, and extend coverage as new products and segments come online.

Apply data science to cost and usage data: Build forecasting models, detect anomalies statistically rather than by threshold alone, and quantify savings opportunities (e.g. storage lifecycle, request-cost patterns) with rigor a spreadsheet can't match.

Build and maintain cost attribution: Tagging policies, cost allocation, and chargeback/showback so engineering teams can see and own their own spend. This is foundational work other savings work depends on.

Automate cost governance: Build automated cost reporting, anomaly detection, and alerting. Write the scripts and infrastructure-as-code (Python, Terraform, Lambda) that enforce cost policy rather than relying on manual review.

Partner with engineering on architecture decisions: Bring cost into the room early, cost-efficiencies are cheaper to get right at design than to retrofit.

Work with Finance on forecasting and reporting: Support budget tracking and financial KPIs; build dashboards and self-serve analytics engineering and finance can both read.

Have strong AWS expertise and working GCP knowledge, including pricing models, billing structures, and cost optimization mechanics.

Have data engineering depth: dbt, BigQuery (or an equivalent modern warehouse), SQL at scale, and data modeling for analytics (dimensional modeling, incremental models, testing).

Have data science fundamentals: statistical forecasting, anomaly detection, and experimentation, and know when a rigorous model beats a rule of thumb.

Have automation and scripting skills: Python, Terraform/ pulumi, Lambda, or Bash.

Are comfortable with cost/billing tooling: AWS Cost Explorer, Cost & Usage Reports, GCP Billing Reports, and BI/dashboarding (we use Hex).

Have experience with, or are comfortable picking up, Linear and Notion as the system of record for tracking and documenting FinOps work.

Experience with a dedicated cloud cost management platform (e.g. CloudZero, Vantage, or similar) is a plus, not required.

Can analyze cost data and present it clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences.

Have prior experience spanning data analytics, data engineering, or data science in a FinOps, cloud cost management, or cloud governance context.

Equity refers to a fair and impartial workplace, aiming to ensure equal growth and advancement opportunities for all employees. This involves amplifying underrepresented voices, addressing unconscious biases, and providing inclusive, culturally competent mental health care.

Inclusion signifies the practice of granting equal access to opportunities and resources for all employees, particularly those who might otherwise be excluded or marginalized. It ensures that everyone feels a sense of belonging, value, support, and respect as an individual.

Belonging reflects the affinity and positive relationships that develop among employees from diverse backgrounds when businesses actively promote diversity, equity, and inclusion in the workplace.

You will develop and pilot new AI-enabled investigatory processes for Clover’s Medicare Advantage business, and own resulting investigations, in collaboration with Clover’s Special Investigations Unit (SIU) and other stakeholders.

Success in this role requires someone sharp, creative, and technically hands-on—someone who does not just use existing analytics tools but builds their own. That might mean writing a script to automate repetitive work, pulling apart a dataset when a standard report falls short, or working with an LLM until it produces something genuinely useful—all with the goal of finding smarter, more effective ways to investigate potential provider fraud.

As a Director, AI-Enabled Fraud Prevention & Investigations, you will:

About Clover: We are reinventing health insurance by combining the power of data with human empathy to keep our members healthier. We always put our members first, and our success as a team is measured by the quality of life of the people we serve. #195. Head of Legal at Kit

Kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

You'll report to our Chief Operating Officer, Brian Bevel, and partner regularly with leaders across product, sales, finance, and people operations. You'll own our core legal work in-house, reduce the need for outside counsel, and know when specialized outside counsel is truly needed.

First year: Help Kit operate at a higher level of legal maturity across privacy, compliance, product counsel, commercial contracts, and security support. Establish durable systems that allow teams to answer common questions independently while escalating higher-risk matters appropriately. Help us treat privacy, data, and compliance as strategic enablers—not just boxes to check—and significantly reduce our reliance on outside counsel for work we can handle effectively in-house.

Deep expertise in data, compliance, and product—this is where you'll spend most of your time.

Strong ability to navigate U.S. and European data privacy laws (e.g., GDPR, CCPA), including familiarity with data controller vs. processor distinctions and how they shape vendor and product decisions.

Ability to translate privacy and compliance requirements into scalable playbooks, templates, intake processes, and self-service guidance

Experience supporting customer security questionnaires and partnering effectively with security, sales, product, and engineering teams

Familiarity with SOC 2 Type II and the legal, privacy, and customer requirements associated with it, even if you haven't directly owned a certification process

Understanding of intellectual property law, especially related to brand, content, and software

Understanding of commercial contracts—you'll become the go-to person for these at Kit.

Clear communicator and trusted advisor—able to simplify complexity and help others make informed decisions

Experience as in-house counsel at a tech company or serving a tech portfolio at a top-tier firm that's well-known for their work with startups (e.g., Fenwick & West, Cooley)

J.D. from an accredited law school in the United States

Active member in good standing of a State Bar Association

Strategic thinker who sees legal as a lever, not a blocker

Deeply curious and business-oriented—you start by understanding the goals, then explore the smartest paths to get there.

Collaborative partner who can navigate conflict productively

Deep belief that creator success is our success—you consider both Kit and our customers in every recommendation

A "how might we" problem-solver who finds creative, business-aligned paths through legal challenges

Needing a team of in-house peers or co-counsel to pressure-test every decision—you'll be our sole in-house legal expert, with outside counsel available as needed

A strongly risk-averse or "no-before-yes" mindset—we need you to help us move, not just stop us from tripping

Thinking in a legal vacuum—if you're not factoring in our goals, numbers, or creators, your advice won't land

Struggling with speed or ownership—if you prefer long timelines or wait to be told what to do, this won't be the right environment. We move quickly and expect people to take initiative, spot problems, and drive solutions.

We're 100% remote with team members across the globe. For this role, we're looking for someone located in the United States.

Kit has standardized salaries based on position, no matter where you live. This role is an individual contributor level 4 ($227,000) or 5 ($252,000). Our other perks and benefits include:

We cover up to $2,100 per month toward medical premiums, with dental and vision premiums fully covered. We offer Health Insurance plans through Aetna

$2,000 equipment allowance for your first two years, $1,000 budget every following two years. Company-provided laptops are issued to every Kit team member and are not included in the equipment budget

Individual learning + development budget ($3,500/year)

Childcare benefit up to $3,000 annually through JOON

Twenty (20) days of paid time off during each year of employment

Paid paid vacation: An after-tax bonus of $1,000 for taking five consecutive days of vacation where you’re fully unplugged from work

Two weeks of paid sick time each year, including mental health + well being days

Twelve (12) weeks paid parental leave and flexible scheduling in your child’s first year

Up to six weeks of paid bereavement leave, medical leave, and disaster after six months of employment, two weeks of each paid leave in your first six months

Winter Break Closure: Kit closes for a week at the end of December, giving everyone a collective break to enjoy the holiday season. Essential support services remain available, with teams coordinating to ensure coverage during this period

Four-week, paid sabbatical after five years with the team

Fantastic in-person or virtual retreats with the team twice a year

A phone screen with our recruiter (30 min)

Panel interview with cross functional stakeholders (60 min)

We're looking for our first Product Operations Manager. Our product team is small, senior, and growing fast, with each PM coming in to establish the foundations of a new part of the business. As the team grows, the work that connects it (how we plan, set and measure goals, keep the roadmap honest, run our rituals, learn from customers, and bring new people up to speed) needs an owner.

This role is that owner. Your customers are the PMs and the head of product, and your job is to make them faster and better at what they do. You won't be inheriting a process manual or enforcing one. You'll be designing how a product team works at the moment it goes from a handful of people to a real organization, inside an engineering culture that values autonomy and only adopts what makes people's lives easier.

see the people you support as customers, and start from their problems rather than from a framework

like building systems from scratch more than maintaining them

would rather remove a meeting than add one

write clearly and enjoy making complicated things legible

are a fast learner, frequently picking up new tools and techniques, including AI

The best way to impress us is by trying LiveKit's product, understanding how we work, and bringing smart thoughts and opinions to the table.

Run the product team's operating cadence. You own the calendar of planning cycles, reviews, and recurring updates: what each one is for, who needs to be there, what goes in, and what comes out. You make sure decisions and follow-ups are captured and visible to everyone who needs them, and you keep retiring or reshaping rituals that stop earning their time.

Own the roadmap as a system. You own how the roadmap is structured, at the right altitude for each audience, from engineering teams to leadership to sales. You make sure it stays current and becomes the place people go to find out what we're building and where it stands.

With our data team, you own the reporting the product team and leadership rely on, and you flag drift early.

Keep the product development playbook. You maintain lightweight shared standards for each step from framing a problem through launch: problem briefs, launch readiness, product stage definitions, release notes. With marketing, you run the internal side of every launch so each one ships with docs, pricing, and GTM ready.

Run the customer insight engine. You own the systems that keep customers close to the product team: a research repository people use, a continuous pipeline of customer conversations set up with sales and success, and a steady synthesis of what we hear from sales, support, surveys, and deals, delivered to the PMs who need it.

Grow the craft of the PM team. You own onboarding for new PMs, ongoing training, and the team's community of practice, and you help shape how we hire and level PMs.

Choose and run the team's tools. You decide how the product team uses its tools, from roadmapping and analytics to AI, and you make sure PMs get real leverage from them.

Be a partner in running the product org. You keep a pulse on where the team is stuck, bring your own point of view on what to fix next, and work with the head of product to make the product org better every quarter.

6+ years of experience, with at least 3 in product operations or a closely related role (chief of staff to a product leader, product program management, product strategy and operations) supporting a product team.

You've built it before. You've designed a product team's operating cadence from scratch at a company that was scaling, not only kept an existing one running.

A force multiplier. You measure your success by what changed for the people you support, not by how much process exists.

A strong writer. Most of what this role produces is read by other people: templates, updates, plans, and documentation.

Data fluent. You're comfortable defining metrics, working in BI tools, and telling a trustworthy number from an untrustworthy one. SQL is a plus.

Technical enough for a developer company. Our customers are developers and our organization is engineering-led. You don't need to write code, but you need to be credible with the people who do.

Influence without authority. Our engineering teams operate with high autonomy. Nothing here works by mandate; it works because it's useful.

Alloy’s platform is complex and managed with high-touch support from Alloy’s Technical Solutions team. Customers that would like to ‘self-serve’ often struggle to build a clear mental model of how Alloy works and why, falling back to Alloy’s support teams to complete even simple tasks. Today, enablement is spread across multiple repositories and handled one-to-one by delivery teams, with inconsistent results. Only a handful of sophisticated and adventurous clients currently achieve a moderate amount of self-sufficiency.

This leader owns customer enablement across Alloy. This is not a technical writing role. It is a role that builds and runs the program behind enablement: capturing knowledge continuously, packaging it for the right audience at the right moment, running hands-on customer training sessions, and measuring what works.

The Customer Enablement Lead will report to the VP of Product Design. From within the Product team they will help fill gaps and challenging areas of the product while creating a powerful feedback loop between customers and designers to decrease those gaps and challenges over time. The Enablement Lead will form strong cross-functional connections with the Support, Delivery, Technical Success, Product Marketing, and Product Operations teams to ensure customers have a seamless and supported experience as they go live and as we release new features.

Alloy operates in a hybrid-work environment. We look to foster collaboration and community by having our local employees onsite three days a week. This role is open to both local and remote candidates in the US.

The initial scope of work for this role will include:

Audit the current state. Evaluate and consolidate existing resources (API docs, help articles, the learning center, in-product help, and delivery-built guides). Work with cross-functional partners to create any missing documentation and “Customer 101” program material.

Outcome: Our AI support bot can answer essentially any customer question. Our delivery teams can pull together the content they need to run tailored training sessions with their customers.

Focus on new Alloy customers and deliver scalable, deployable training and content for repeatable implementations. Structure material so clients can self-pace from foundational to advanced. Target key user personas so they learn the features critical to their respective day-to-day.

Outcome: Clients understand and use what they bought, and are aware of what else Alloy offers. Additionally they know where to look for additional guidance via documentation, AI support chat, and other escalation channels.

When Alloy builds a material new feature or capability, map what each client segment and persona needs to know, when, and why, from pre-sales through go-live and ongoing use, and make it part of how products are sold, launched, and delivered.

Outcome: a shared view of our friction points and what areas currently drag the most on our bottom line.

Collect feedback after every release, rollout, and training. Give Product, Design, and Delivery a shared view of where clients get stuck, and drive alignment on whether each gap is best solved by product, technical solutions, or enablement, including interim fixes.

Outcome: Product, Design, and Delivery share one view of enablement gaps and who owns them. The design team gets critical insight continuously, addressing customer confusion directly in the product, helping reduce the surface area for documentation over time.

Onboarding into Alloy, learning the product yourself, existing resource audit, gap analysis, start filling documentation gaps with SME and tooling support, and deliver a consolidation plan.

Initial enablement ‘package’ in beta for first client feedback via early hands-on training sessions.

Initial enablement funnel for core segments deployed and documentation gap filling has demonstrated a measurable increase in AI support ticket resolution. Iteration on the enablement package incorporating early feedback.

Enablement package is ‘production ready’ and universally rolled out (client-facing teams are ready to deliver training using the material). Feedback loop with product and design solidified. The product release enablement funnel is operational as part of new feature releases. Seeing measurable improvements in some areas of self-service and legacy support ticket theme avoidance.

We’re looking for someone who can take ambiguous, messy, business-critical infrastructure problems and turn them into pragmatic systems, tools, standards, and written guidance that scale with the company and empower teams to go faster.

Designing and implementing cloud governance across AWS and GCP, including identity, account organization, access controls, and guardrails.

Building reusable infrastructure and building blocks using Infrastructure as Code (IaC), enabling teams to provision and manage infrastructure safely and consistently.

Creating self-service capabilities that reduce organizational friction and let engineers move more quickly within sensible boundaries.

Owning resource governance and visibility: management tagging, a trustworthy inventory of what exists and who owns it, and consistent cross-account billing data.

Developing reusable security primitives, including secrets storage, KMS, certificate management, token vending, direct service-to-service authentication, mTLS, and related platform services.

Owning cloud-level network and operational primitives: IP address management, DNS, and health signals such as service-limit and quota alerting.

Combining software engineering with hands-on operations and total ownership: building, deploying, monitoring, troubleshooting, and improving what you own.

Establishing and sharing cloud engineering best practices through documentation, internal tooling, examples, and enablement.

#224. Legion: Principal Product Manager, Agentic AI

Legion is building AI agents that carry out workforce management work, not agents that describe it.

Much of what is presented as AI in workforce management today is a conversational layer over an existing scheduling screen. The more substantial problem — software that reasons over demand, labor regulation, and employee preferences, then acts, with a person in the loop wherever the stakes require one — remains unsolved across the category. Legion intends to solve it, and this role leads the product work to get there.

You will take an agent surface from operational research through specification, prototype, evaluation, and enterprise deployment, working hands-on throughout. You will work closely with Legion's AI Lab engineers and with our CEO, who is engaged in this work daily.

Agent definition. Determine what an agent is responsible for, which tools it may call, what it must escalate, what it must never do, and what a manager sees when it acts. These decisions affect employee pay and legal compliance. Much of this work is pre-launch, so you will shape the direction rather than inherit it.

Problem selection. The hardest judgment in agentic product work is identifying which workflows suit an agent and which do not. You will spend substantial time inside customer operations — district managers, store managers, labor operations, frontline employees — and return with a ranked, defensible view of where an agent creates measurable value and where it does not.

The human-in-the-loop contract. Scheduling decisions affect income, childcare arrangements, and legal protections. For each agent action you will define where autonomy is appropriate, the escalation thresholds, how a manager overrides the system, what is logged, and how a compliance team audits the outcome. Legion treats this as a first-class design problem.

Build quality. You are accountable for what ships, not for what was specified. That means staying engaged through implementation: reviewing the build against the specification as it comes together, using the product yourself before anyone else is asked to, joining bug triage and design review, catching drift from intent while it is still cheap to correct, and holding a release when the quality is not there. Our customers experience the build, not the document. A well-written specification that produced a product managers do not trust is failed product work, and we assess it that way.

Evaluation. Build and maintain the evaluation sets that determine whether an agent is ready to ship and whether it is degrading in production — writing the cases, reviewing failure traces, setting the pass criteria. You will be the person who holds a release when the demonstration is persuasive and the evaluation is not.

Specifications. Legion uses Functional Requirements Documents as its ground-truth specification layer; release notes, enablement material, and sales content are generated from maintained specifications rather than reconstructed from code or institutional memory. Write FRDs that meet that standard and keep them accurate after release. A specification is where the work begins, not where your responsibility ends.

Commercialization. Partner with go-to-market on packaging, metering, pricing inputs, and field readiness. Agentic products raise difficult commercial questions — what unit to meter, what a customer is paying for when software performs work a person previously did — and you will be expected to hold a considered position on them.

Design-partner delivery. Lead agent deployments with large enterprise design partners: scoping the pilot, establishing success criteria before it begins, joining failure reviews, and determining what becomes generally available and what remains bespoke.

Legion is looking for a product manager who builds, rather than one who directs others who build. In a typical week, this role involves:

We recognize that this is a demanding technical bar for a product role. It reflects what the work actually requires.

Our process includes a practical exercise: a sanitized workforce management problem, for which candidates produce an agent design — scope, tools, failure modes, human-in-the-loop contract, and evaluation plan — together with a working prototype they built themselves, using any model provider they prefer. The exercise is then discussed with the people the candidate would work alongside. We weigh it heavily, and we compensate candidates for the time.

#250. Upgrade: AI Experience Engineer (Conversational AI)

About the Role:An AI Experience Engineer owns the full lifecycle of the journeys our customers have with Upgrade's AI agent on chat, voice and email: creation, optimization, edge case handling and containment growth. They build journeys in Sierra's no-code tooling, partner with Upgrade's product groups to bring their servicing flows to the agent, and are accountable for whether the agent resolves the customer's issue safely, accurately and without a human.

We are hiring an AI Experience Engineer to own Upgrade's customer-facing AI agent. You will sit between engineering, product and customer operations. You will turn servicing workflows, such as making a payment, checking loan details, updating an address or enabling autopay, into production journeys and keep improving them after launch. You will build and own the journeys end to end, from first draft to steady state. The work is part builder, part analyst: design the flow, handle the edge cases, read the transcripts, and keep raising containment. Containment, CSAT, transfer quality and hallucination rate are your metrics.

Within your first year, you will own a portfolio of journeys across products (Personal Loans, Card, BNPL, HELOC, Deposits) and help set the standards for how Upgrade builds, tests and ships AI experiences.

Sierra Agent Studio (no-code journeys), Sierra simulations and conversation analytics, GraphQL and REST APIs (as journey tools), Genesys (contact center handoff), SumoLogic, Grafana, SQL, Javascript/Typescript, Claude and other LLM tools.

• Journey creation: Design and build Sierra journeys in Agent Studio for chat, voice and email, from discovery with operations through production rollout

• Optimization: Review transcripts, recordings and analytics every week, find where conversations fail or transfer, and ship fixes to journey logic, instructions and knowledge

• Edge case handling: Map the unhappy paths (failed payments, mismatched identity, delinquent accounts, unsupported requests) and make sure each ends in a correct answer or a clean handoff

• Containment: Own containment and CSAT targets per journey, run staged rollouts (1% → 100%), and prioritize the work that moves those numbers most

• Product partnership: Work with product groups (Personal Loans, Card, BNPL, Deposits) to scope new journeys, keep journeys current as products change, and define the APIs the agent needs

• Safety and compliance: Apply tiered authentication and step-up verification, verbatim compliance language and guardrails against hallucination and off-policy answers

• Handoffs: Design transfers to human agents in Genesys with accurate summaries and auth context

• Testing: Build simulation and regression suites so every journey change ships with evidence it did not break existing behavior

• Monitoring: Watch latency, errors and drop-offs in SumoLogic and Grafana, and own the alerts

As our Compliance Manager, you will own and drive Sourcegraph’s governance, risk, and compliance program, with a primary focus on compliance. This is a highly cross-functional role that works closely with Security, Engineering, IT, Legal, People, Sales, and other teams across the company.

You will be responsible for maintaining and evolving our compliance program, including owning certifications such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001 and preparing Sourcegraph for additional frameworks as the business grows. You are comfortable operating independently, getting into the details, and doing the work yourself while coordinating with stakeholders across the organization. You understand that frameworks such as SOC 2 and ISO 27001 define requirements but often leave significant flexibility in how an organization satisfies them, and you know how to translate those requirements into controls that fit the business.

You are also comfortable working with technical teams and modern cloud environments. You can understand enough about infrastructure, systems, access controls, software development, and security processes to ask the right questions and effectively translate between auditors and technical teams.

As a Senior Software Engineer, Backend on Camunda’s Distributed Systems team, you’ll help build and evolve the durable, highly available, horizontally scalable streaming platform that underpins Camunda 8’s Orchestration Cluster and powers mission‑critical processes for customers around the world.

As part of the Distributed Systems team, you will work on technically challenging and rewarding projects, such as expanding on our multi-Raft implementation, our SWIM-based cluster membership algorithm, or high performance network and disk I/O pipelines.

At Camunda, we approach engineering in a holistic manner. As such, you will form strong partnerships with product management, design, QA, and sales, and work with your peers to not only deliver but directly influence the evolution of our platform to meet our customer’s needs.

Design, build, and maintain backend services for the distributed streaming platform that powers the foundation for Camunda 8’s orchestration capabilities, ensuring durability, high availability, and horizontal scalability.

Design and implement developer and operator tooling that makes it easier to understand, troubleshoot, and safely operate a complex distributed system in production environments.

7+ years of professional experience as a software engineer, with a strong focus on backend systems and/or distributed systems.

Proven experience leading medium‑to‑large engineering initiatives (roughly 3+ months), breaking down ambiguous problems, writing clear solution designs and project plans, coordinating with multiple teams, and driving predictable delivery.

Hands‑on experience building and maintaining highly concurrent, data‑intensive software, with a deep understanding of low‑level network and disk I/O (for example, throughput, latency, backpressure, batching, and failure modes).

Demonstrated ability to work autonomously and navigate ambiguity – you are comfortable taking on problems you haven’t solved before, breaking them down into concrete steps, and driving them to completion with minimal supervision.

Strong communication and collaboration skills in a remote‑first environment: you tailor explanations to your audience, translate business requirements into actionable technical work with Product, and help teams reach clear, decisive outcomes with minimal churn.

Experience building workflow automation or process orchestration software.

Experience with distributed systems algorithms or protocols such as Raft, Paxos, SWIM, and/or CRDTs.

Strong familiarity with the observability pillars (logging, metrics, tracing) and how to integrate observability into the development and incident lifecycle, ideally including experience with L3 support and on‑call.

Deep knowledge of the Java Virtual Machine, especially its memory model and performance characteristics in highly concurrent, data‑intensive workloads.
